Ed. note: The Graduate Center is a buzzing hive of collective study. One gang in particular, however, has stood out for its timeliness: the Project 2025 reading group. Over the summer, a dozen or so students and faculty came together to study the Heritage Foundation’s playbook for Trump 2.0, officially titled “Mandate for Leadership: The Conservative Promise.” Weighing in at 920 pages of dry policy proposals and ideological cautioning, reading this document is a worthwhile (and grueling) feat. What follows is a lightly edited interview with the group’s founder, Phoebe Myers, on collaborative inquiry, Project 2025, and the rolling displeasures of this particular text. 

 

This is something of an unusual graduate school reading group. Can you tell us a bit about how this idea came about and how the group came together? Why did you see it as imperative to collectively study Project 2025?

 

I had the thought to create a group of some kind while in Dr. Eric Lott’s class “Introduction to American Studies” in the Spring of 2025. Project 2025 was kind of a spectre looming behind much of what we discussed in that class: especially its effects on US policy and ideology. I knew a few major Project 2025 items from news headlines, but in this class, I realized that there was a lot I was missing  not having read the document myself. 

 

Particularly, I thought that reading Project 2025 as an ideological artifact could be useful in opposing its application. Knowing the content of Project 2025, I felt, was only half the picture. I was interested to see if anything about it as a text, its structure or language, could be of use in better understanding the rightwing ideology, what within it was enticing to the right, and how to fight against it. I knew the document was about 900 pages long and while part of the idea of a collective study was knowing I would burn out on my own while reading it, the main desire was to reach folks from different perspectives outside just the English department. The text itself has policies impacting vastly different areas of American society, and I think the left might miss crucial insights if we only engage with the sections that most directly impact our disciplines/work/lives. A collective study with people with backgrounds in sociology, music, and psychology as well as English was invaluable to me in getting new perspectives from the text I would have otherwise missed. 

 

What are the points the group found most salient? For example, what were the “issues” most frequently harped upon? And aside from the most repeated topics, what seemed to be the most vanguard positions taken—the most radical departures from what we generally understand as American conservatism? 

 

One primary debate that arose from the document was how united, or not, the right actually is. At first glance, it seemed a heroic feat that about 300 people came together to co-create Project 2025. It was a bit scary to imagine a right so united they were able to put aside internal disagreements and present a “unified” policy proposal. We discussed how impossible it felt to imagine 300 leftists agreeing on a cohesive policy proposal without infighting. However, the situation is nuanced. For example, though it wasn’t explicitly described in the text as a disagreement, we noted how there were differing viewpoints presented between authors on the authoritarian side of the spectrum and those with a more anti-statist position.  In the foreword, Kevin D. Roberts advocated for small government, but a major throughline of the following sections were all advising federal departments to centralize power in the executive branch through replacing “career bureaucrats” with political appointees and make drastic spending cuts on “waste” outside of the executive branch. Besides the major point of hypocrisy within the text advocating for  small government while strengthening the reach and power of the executive branch, there were other moments of disagreement between the authors like whether working on the Sabbath should be disincentivized by the government (this was presented structurally as a disagreement, with an opposing viewpoint being labeled as an “alternative view”). 

 

While there were moments of hope where we saw chinks in the armor of the united right, there were radical positions taken as well which our group were slightly surprised by. One was the promotion of child labor, with recommendations to lower age restrictions to work and that, with parental consent, some young adults should be able to work in “more dangerous” occupations (595). 

 

The economic and cultural factions of American conservatism have sometimes held an uneasy partnership. How much of the document struck you as libertarian laissez faire capitalism and how much struck you as Christian nationalist moralism? Did Project 2025 manage to synthesize these positions in any way or were these aporias elided?

 

This was the subject of some of our discussions. Particularly the question of how influential is Christianity, really, to these policy recommendations?  I believe our consensus was that Project 2025 did not manage to synthesize these contradictions, with one point of tension being this question of working on the Sabbath as I mentioned before. Our group was leaning towards the conception that, though libertarian laissez faire capitalism is ultimately driving the bus of the right wing agenda, the authors of Project 2025 likely felt pressure to connect these policies with the right’s Christian nationalist base. Certainly, the Christian nationalist moralism was especially apparent in language and policies centered on “protecting” the nuclear family—imagined as a heterosexual, cis-gendered, able-bodied, married couple with children. 

 

What were the most frightening parts of the program? 

 

It is a bit hard to choose the most frightening parts of the program. For one, calls for the CDC to be muzzled and unable to enforce policy recommendations such as mask or vaccine mandates is frightening given the ongoing realities of COVID-19 and the possibilities of future epidemics or pandemics. Recommending extreme restrictions in abortion access were also alarming, such as ending taxpayer funding of Planned Parenthood and redirecting the funds to women’s “health centers” that do not provide abortions. From an environmental perspective, there was a direct call for climate-change research to be disbanded within the federal government amongst a plethora of environmentally disastrous policy recommendations. The restriction of rights of women and LGBTQIA+ people were also distressing, such as the suggestion that no public education employee should be able to use any pronoun to address a student different from their biological sex according to school records without written permission from the students’ parents. 

 

Much of the program has been denounced as impracticable or, if attained, nightmarish in consequence. Was there anything the group read in the document that gave pause and made you reconsider the seriousness of the playbook? 

 

Certainly, some of these would be (and are) nightmarish if implemented. We did reference a website, project2025.observer/en, which is a community-driven initiative to track the policies suggested in Project 2025 to see which have been implemented so far under the Trump administration and which are in-progress. As of now, they’re tracking 318 policy objectives, and of those objectives, 48% have already been completed and implemented by the Trump administration. This in and of itself made us really think about the seriousness of the playbook, given that so many of its objectives have already been put in place. 

 

Do you think that right-wingers are reading leftist documents in this way? Do you think that the left errs by not having documents like Project 2025 from the left position? 

 

To be frank, I’m struggling to think of what documents the left has that would be comparable to this in terms of scope and with the credentials that Project 2025 had. 140 of the authors of Project 2025 worked in the Trump administration or for his campaign, and the Heritage Foundation (which created Project 2025) has extensive influence on U.S. public policy. Much of Project 2025 commented on the Heritage Foundation’s long legacy of creating these documents. Project 2025 is far from their first document suggesting policies for an incoming conservative president. Since 1973, they’ve been creating policy guides like Project 2025, an entire genre they call “Mandate for Leadership.” They made a mandate of recommendations for Ronald Reagan, many of which he implemented, and that legacy is still a point of pride for the Heritage Foundation. 

 

In our group, we talked a lot about his lack of a comparable policy document on the left. We agreed that the left could benefit from attempting to create a similar document. One session was particularly fruitful where we talked about how important it is for the left to clearly identify our policies to attract voters. It’s not enough to simply position ourselves as anti-Trump or even anti-Project 2025. The left should not try to shift its policies to reach certain voting demographics, but focus on clearly articulating their own position, and that clarity will attract new voting demographics. We actually talked about how the points of tension within Project 2025 indicate they are trying to appeal to too many groups which could present an opportunity for the left to create a more united and impactful document. 

 

Since we are situated at CUNY, how much of this document speaks to the current moment of repression on higher ed? What else do the Heritage Foundation and Trump Administration have in store for institutions of study? 

 

We’ve been seeing the impacts of many policy recommendations from Project 2025 on higher education already. Particularly the dismantling of the Department of Education and threats of withholding federal funding to institutions who teach critical race theory or incorporate D.E.I.; as well as the cancellation of federal NEA research grants for projects concerning climate justice, critical race or gender studies, among other topics. These threats have all been rightfully covered extensively by the media. 

 

One potentially underexamined threat to higher education we noticed in our group was the suggestion that universities begin to compete to suggest policy plans to the federal government rather than having governmental agencies (like the CDC) make policy recommendations. This “competition” would be tied to accessing funds if their policy proposals are chosen. While Project 2025 states this would mitigate the risk of “unaccountable” bureaucrats making policy recommendations, following their main argument that these bureaucrats should be replaced by political appointees that Trump can hand-select, outsourcing policy recommendations to universities still contains risk. One potential risk being that, as universities become more dependent on following Trump’s policies to access funds, they may solely suggest policies that align with whatever his administration wants, or is deemed to want. Or, the Trump administration could simply choose the “winner” of the competition to be whatever aligns with his administration. While the possibility of universities making policy recommendations could seem at first like a good thing, it’s worth looking at the potential downsides as well.

Ed. note: We sat down with one of the members of the Fired Four, a group of four adjunct professors at CUNY who were unceremoniously jettisoned by the administration a few months ago by non-reappointment. To maintain some degree of plausible deniability—the administration has already shown itself to be capable of reprisal—we have chosen to keep the names anonymous. 

 

To start off, what were the conditions of your non-appointment? How did you and the other three adjuncts realize you were all in the same boat? Was it purely deductive reasoning?

 

It’s important to place our firing in a political context. There has been a historic uprising of students and university workers on the side of Palestine, creating a movement that questions Zionism, imperialism and the investments our universities have in Israel—as well as the very idea that universities should be run as businesses. This has been met with a furious bipartisan reaction, including police brutality against protesters, suspensions and firings. Trump has only escalated these attacks on free speech, the movement for Palestine, the left and especially international students. Our firings are intertwined in this political scenario of united struggle and repression.

 

On the specifics of my firing: This was different for me than from the other members of the Fired Four. I was supposed to be teaching a summer class when I received an email that said I had been fired for “just cause for conduct unbecoming of staff.” I emailed back and asked, “What conduct?” Then I received a reply with the phrase “conduct unbecoming of the staff” highlighted and no other information. 

 

About 2-3 weeks after that, the other three adjuncts received notices that they were not being re-appointment. A few days later, I received one too. All of the chairs of our departments were seeking to reappoint us. In all of our departments we had very high student and faculty observations. Actually, in one of my departments 95% of students said that they would recommend my course to a friend. 

 

Until 2020, the departments had final say on reappointments – now it has to get signed off by HR. And these letters came from HR precisely, overruling recommendations from chairs to reappoint us. When our dept. chairs asked, no answer was forthcoming. This is unprecedented. The chairs in our departments cannot recall a time this has ever happened. 

 

In my personal case, however, since I was first fired, they had to give me a reason. We filed a Taylor Law Information Request and received three charges: 1) in a political flyer, I, students and other faculty used CUNY in the title; 2) the flyer contained a QR-code that allowed people to get more information; 3) because I received a 5$ donation from another faculty member for relevant materials. Those were the factors considered “conduct unbecoming.” There are dozens, if not hundreds of examples of faculty and students engaging in the same activities. It is clear that I, and the three other faculty, are being singled out for our politics. 

 

This was for the summer. Brooklyn College then specified I was “non-reappointed” for the fall, along with the others, and the reason for this was never given. Since we are adjuncts—even though we have been teaching at Brooklyn College; personally I’ve been here for five years—we were not owed an explanation by the administration. Here the institution really capitalizes on the precarity in the rules surrounding the firing of adjuncts, claiming we don’t deserve any due process.

If it sounds confusing, it’s because it is. But to be clear, Brooklyn College is claiming I was only fired for conduct unbecoming for the summer and then in the fall I was non-reappointed for an unspecified reason. The other three have been non-reappointed for the fall – and for all four of us, over the heads of our chairs who have been very supportive. 

 

All four of us are involved in the pro-Palestine movement at CUNY, and we were all active in the PSC union. At Brooklyn College on May 8, 2025, where students launched an action seeking divestment, setting up tents in the quad. BC President Michelle Anderson refused to meet with students and eventually called the police onto campus to brutalize the students. Ten were arrested; one tased. One of my former students was punched in the face by an NYPD officer and thrown to the ground. Many faculty participated in protecting students and declaring support for divestment, against genocide. Brooklyn College clearly is embarking on what the PSC calls an “ideological purge” of pro-Palestinian elements on campus, and is doing so at the expense of the right to free speech and the right to protest. Five full-time faculty members and one staff member who were present at the protest are also being investigated by Brooklyn College and at least eight students across CUNY have been suspended, including Hadeeqa Arzoo Malik from City College. 

 

Just a few weeks after we were fired, the CUNY Chancellor testified before the House Education and Workforce Committee, where he offered the four of us up as a gift to the far-right in an attempt to prove that he is disciplining pro-Palestine professors. He mentioned one of us by name and stated that four faculty had been disciplined, alongside multiple students. In this hearing, it was clear that the right isn’t just coming for the Palestine movement, but for academic freedom in general, for our unions and defunding our universities. We are the canaries in the coal mine for a much greater onslaught against our basic rights. 

 

What has the response of the CUNY community at large been to this firing? How has the PSC responded? 

 

The outpouring of support has been heartening. The PSC has taken up our cause in a campaign to oppose what they call an “ideological purge” and have designated “The New McCarthyism.” In a rare moment of consensus, the union delegate assembly voted unanimously to condemn the firings. And folks are mobilized. This campaign includes many movement for Palestine folks; folks from the PSC, especially the Brooklyn College chapter; folks from the Fight to Win caucus; SJPs and CUNY For Palestine; and also includes the Brooklyn College Student Union, as well as students, faculty and staff that haven’t been politically active before. Even folks outside CUNY including the Rutgers Adjunct Union, as well as education-related groups, have been supportive. 

 

We have a group chat of over 250 people and have tabled on over 10 campuses at this point. Faculty, staff, and students united in distributing information about the Fired Four, as well as information about the suspension of Hadeeqa, the head of City College’s SJP, among others. We have held many demonstrations—one in the pouring rain at Brooklyn, one at the Grad Center, one at CUNY central. We’ve had panels including with the esteemed academic Ellen Schrecker, who writes about McCarthyism. We have had a “wear red” solidarity day. We fliered outside Zohran Mamdani and Bernie Sanders’ event at Brooklyn College and it was important that Zohran spoke out about the Fired Four. 

 

We have had “Angry Hours” where campaign members socialize and confer about what is going on. We have t-shirts for our campaign to get reinstated. We have an Instagram with over a thousand followers called @reinstatecunyfiredfour – follow us!

 

This has become a lightning rod of politicization for the CUNY community to resist Trumpism and the right-wing lurch towards authoritarianism and the attacks on the bipartisan assault on the movement for Palestine. 

 

Do you consider this response commensurate to the administration’s aggression? 

 

In order to fight to get our jobs back, we will have to continue to strengthen our fight from below. It’s important work what people are doing now: tabling, organizing protests, getting resolutions passed in our unions, demanding that politicians like Zohran speak up in favor of the Fired Four. I especially want to shout out the Brooklyn College student union, whose first meeting of the semester was to do an art-build for the Fired Four, an incredible expression of student and worker solidarity.  If we get our jobs back, it will be because of the movement that is already in motion. For me, it is also really important to get new people in and involved in the struggle. The No Kings march was just last weekend, and there were over 200,000 people in the streets of NYC – it’s clear that people beyond the “usual” crowd are becoming politicized. The question is how to bring them into the struggle, how to mobilize – for the pro-Palestine movement; against the New McCarthyism, for immigrants rights – and how to establish new democratic formations to continue the fight. It’s essential that we continue the struggle against the continued brutality in Palestine, for divestment and for a free Palestine. And we must connect the fight against repression to the fight for immigrants’ rights and against all of Trump’s attacks. 

 

Taking a historical view, since this issue is called “The New McCarthyism,” do you see your firing as part of a larger tendency in American society? Have we put too much faith in the university as a guardian of “free speech”?

 

Yes – the parallels are quite alarming. “Conduct unbecoming” was the favored way to discipline people at CUNY in the old McCarthyism. At Brooklyn College, nine students were suspended for publishing their paper The Vanguard for “conduct unbecoming”; they responded by publishing under another name, The Draugnav, which is vanguard spelled backwards, and were again suspended for “conduct unbecoming.” This tired phrase is now used as a bludgeon against the left, on the pro-Palestine movement, on the pro-immigration movement. 

 

CUNY is not a far-right administration. CUNY has in fact positioned itself as a progressive institution. The point however is that, in the midst of a general rightward drift, the downgrading of the US empire, and more generally the crisis of American capital, the center cannot hold. And so the university, the class interest of the university, the political interest of the university, is now laid bare. Thus we have a situation in which members of the university—administrators, presidents, chancellors—who genuinely consider themselves progressive also fight tooth and nail to maintain investment in the state of Israel. Moreover, they want to maintain a university that doesn’t question the fact that universities are run like businesses that hyper-exploit their adjunct faculty. That is the university system we are in.

 

While a movement to oppose both imperial complicity and economic precarity within the university grows, we are met with drastic crack-downs; and we find the supposedly progressive institution of CUNY operating on the same side as the Republicans who also want to crack down on us. They do the dirty work of the far right. And so I don’t think we can have any faith in university administrators, and we can’t fight to simply return to the neoliberal status quo that was based in universities that have investments in Israel, that run universities like businesses, that keep students mired in debt and exploit workers. That’s not the vision we should have. 

 

What this makes clear is that the people who have the best interests of the university in their heart are the faculty that are involved in the movement. In that sense, we have to question who runs the university. Should it be a chancellor who makes hundreds of thousands of dollars? Or should it be the students, the workers, the staff that actually make the university run? It’s clear that this moment of crisis has produced an alternative vision of the university that protects our right to teach against the status quo. But importantly it should be by and for the community, by and for the working class students, the immigrant students and students of color, that comprise the university. Here we are in a moment of crisis that has produced a convergence between the pro-Palestine movement and the left under the vision of a free CUNY – in fact, a CUNY where students receive a stipend to go to school – and a CUNY run by faculty, staff and students in the service of working-class and oppressed people, not in service of ruling-class interests, or the interests of US imperialism.

by Liz Janoff

 

The recent documentary Drop Dead City revisits and expands a circumstance we are fatally familiar with: austerity. Telling the story of the New York 1975 fiscal crisis, the film sketches, in full color, the history of how we arrived at the meager public funds of today. In 16 mm footage, men in suits and ties with expressive faces, sideburns, giant eyebrows, and thick-rimmed glasses sit at conference tables that seem much too big or in expansive dining halls trying to figure out how exactly the city’s deficit estimation could be off by several billion dollars. Mayor Abraham Beame, all of five-foot-two and surrounded by much-taller men, appears in the film again and again looking absolutely gutted, as he takes the fall for this decade-in-the-making financial collapse, with sinister implications for a new era that, despite his role in its making, seemed distant from his own postwar epoch. 

 

Directed by Peter Yost and Michael Rohatyn, the documentary builds slowly toward the day of October 30, 1975, when The Daily News famously ran the front-page headline, “Ford to New York: Drop Dead”––but in reality, Ford never really said that. Interviewed in the film, Ford’s communications director, David Gergen, who was in charge of putting together the hardline speech, recalls still being shocked that what Ford actually said hadn’t been watered down. Through television scan lines, we see the footage of Ford standing at the podium in front of the National Press Club, where he announces affirmatively: 

 

The time has come for all Americans to consider how the problems of New York and the hard decisions they demand foreshadow and focus upon potential problems for all governments. Responsibility for New York’s financial problems is being left on the front doorstep of the federal government, unwanted and abandoned by its real parents. I can tell you and tell you now that I am prepared to veto any bill that has as its purpose, a federal bailout of New York City to prevent a default.

 

The speech is a fundamental part of the narrative of the 1975 crisis, which led to the layoffs of over 40,000 city employees and the end of free tuition at CUNY, but it is also crucial to the documentary’s looming message: that the cuts that resulted from the city’s many years of fiscal mismanagement were not simply inevitable; they were a definitive political decision as New York was refashioned as a testing ground for austerity. Ford would lose the election to Jimmy Carter as a result of the “drop dead” speech––as on-screen text at the end of the film reminds us––but the conservative appeals, led by Ronald Regan, to shrink governments, union power, and all municipal services were, of course, just ramping up. New York’s debt “failures” became a template in the rear view.

 

This is also the perspective put forth explicitly in the 2017 book Fear City: New York’s Fiscal Crisis and the Rise of Austerity by Katherine Phillips-Fein, one of the many people thanked by the directors in the documentary’s credits. Using New York as an object-lesson, Phillips-Fein holds that, in the municipal bankruptcies of the past two decades, “the long-standing tensions that create fiscal crises seem to vanish from consideration in the heat and drama of the moment.” Put on view in the film, for example, are the well-documented factors of suburban investment: white flight, deindustrialization, recession, and the self-interest of the banks who took advantage of municipal debt expansion, profiting at every turn. As everything began to crumble in 1975, however, these forces and the bad actors that refused accountability (the film singles out U.S. Secretary of Treasury, William Simon, for one) became obscured by New York’s immediate and mind-boggling accounting issues, in which, as one of the film’s interviewees exclaims, “Everybody had stuff in drawers” and “There were no fucking books!” 

 

Archival footage displays the fury of protests as the ax drops on every indispensable municipal service the city has to offer, from hospitals to schools to firemen, interspersed with clips of speeches by the city’s union presidents, who were then all powerful––a status that the bankers who took the city’s budget hostage worked to reverse. Al Shanker of the teacher’s union in particular, described in the film as “not just like a god; he was a god,” is the only union leader to hold out until the last hours, the last minutes before the city’s default, refusing and then conceding to sign union pensions over to the Municipal Assistance Committee. Nicknamed “Big MAC,” this was the infamous committee of investment bankers, led by Felix Rohatyn––the father of one of the film’s directors––that was put in place by the state to “sort out” New York City’s fiscal affairs. Rohatyn is portrayed somewhat confusingly as a hero-villain, described as a tenacious dealmaker, apparently passionate about people and city government, but responsible for getting everyone at the negotiating table (with the signal exception of the banks) to “give something up.” 

 

***

 

We witness budget cut after budget cut set to quick bursts of orchestral music or slow piano until one major climax of the documentary when Donna Shalala, treasurer of Big MAC in 1975, recounts the protests that ensued from their decision to charge tuition at CUNY. Sitting with a coffee mug that reads “New York” in small twee letters, she explains, “Destroying one of the clear identities of the city, free tuition for any New York city resident, it was just devastating.” This is followed by a short clip of a protest outside Hunter College (the students chant “they say cut back, we say fight back”), which today dispenses a profound feeling of déjà vu. Though the documentary does show the outrage in the city against Big MAC, as a completely unelected committee of banker–negotiators, there is something altogether too cozy in the film about the city and state bureaucrats sitting in nicely furnished rooms as they recall the unpleasant butchering of New York’s entire community infrastructure; as if to say, what were we supposed to do? 

For this reason, Drop Dead City should be watched in tandem with Tighten Your Belts, Bite the Bullet, the 1980 documentary on the fiscal crisis directed by James Gaffney, Martin Lucas, and Jonathan Miller. Made just five years after New York’s near-bankruptcy, it not only paints the problem as a product of then growing neoliberal economics, that of Regan and Milton Friedman, who both get cameos in Drop Dead, but likens the Big MAC situation, in the words of economist David Gordon, to “a palace coup.” In addition to Big MAC, New York State had created Emergency Financial Control Board (EFCB), which was given the power to veto budget items and labor contracts; as Gordon explains: “They simply said, we won’t loan the city any more money if you don’t let us take power away from you. And so they did it.”

Tighten Your Belts, Bite the Bullet specifically compares the fiscal crisis of New York City to that of Cleveland in 1978, where Dennis Kucinich, Cleveland mayor at the time, refused to let Cleveland Trust blackmail the city by forcing the sale of their public electric company Muny Light (now Cleveland Public Power). Unlike New York, Cleveland did default, and the mayor brought Cleveland citizens to a vote, as they opted to raise income taxes and preserve Muny Light––a decision that in retrospect would save residents large sums of money. In other words, as the documentary argues, there is nothing inescapable (or even practical) about short-term austerity. However, as Drop Dead City submits, New York City was, in the eyes of many, too economically important to go bankrupt. So with taxes from Albany, severe union concessions, money from the feds, and finally some money from Ford, the city narrowly missed falling off another financial cliff; but the municipal cuts nevertheless set a brutal precedent. In 1980, Tighten Your Belts, Bite the Bullet warned other cities facing default: don’t “rollover for the banks” like New York did. 

With footage sourced from over two-dozen archives, Drop Dead City is a masterful mashup of life in New York in 1975 that also translates to a kind of sentimental love letter to the city, the upbeat “Back in the New York Groove” playing over the film’s credits. Ironically, the on-screen text of the credits also imparts that the very last MAC bond was paid off in the financial-crises-ridden year of 2008, conjuring yet another fiscal whirlpool. The whiplash between fun footage and its devastating ramifications in the film is dizzying. As it stands, CUNY tuition should be free; but also, 1975 should light up in our minds anytime we navigate CUNY and its discontents, the result of governance by debt—by blackmail; by callousness; by unelected review boards; by bankers; by unnecessary fiscal mayhem. Fifty years later, the lesson of the fiscal crisis isn’t just to show us the blueprints of American austerity, but rather that alternative policies are and have always been possible.

by William O’Neill

Two ore tankers go aground in the mud of St. Clair, Canada.
A coffee plot is uncovered in Brazil.
Russian tanks tool up, roll toward East Berlin.
[…]
The electrical sign reading AMERICA THE HOPE OF THE WORLD has been altered to AMERICA THE DOPE OF THE WORLD, and metamorphosing a letter at a time right before the eyes of astonished passersby, becomes:

AMERICA THE ROPE OF THE WORLD
AMERICA THE RAPE OF THE WORLD

What’s happening?!?

Robert Coover’s The Public Burning (1977) is a postmodern historical novel which depicts the three days leading up to the 1953 execution of the Rosenbergs, from the perspective of then-Vice President Richard Nixon. But already this phrase, postmodern historical novel, has thrown us off balance—isn’t the defining symptom of the postmodern its “loss of historicity”? Jameson’s prime example of the postmodern historical novel, E.L. Doctorow’s Ragtime (1975) supposedly shows, in its style, down to the sentence, the impossibility of representing the historical past, other than through free-floating stereotypes and half-remembered figures like Houdini or J.P. Morgan. But Coover’s style is wildly different to Doctorow’s (whose own novel on the Rosenbergs, The Book of Daniel (1971), is stylistically even further away from The Public Burning, taking the Rosenbergs’ son as narrator, now a graduate student reckoning with his childhood). The form is clearly indebted to high modernism: a panoramic prologue; four chapters of Nixon taking place in real-time; an intermezzo between each, the first Eisenhower’s inaugural address broken into free verse, the second a dramatic dialogue, the third an opera; and an epilogue whose genuinely shocking contents I won’t betray here. 

The Public Burning’s panorama is not the arm’s-length suspended viewpoint of Ragtime, but some kind of synthesised poetic voice of “the media”: a technique with traces in Malraux and Joyce, but only possible in the mise en scene of postwar New York, “awash in newsprint.” Such breathless synchronic sweep is only possible in a situation like that of the Rosenbergs. The contemporary relevance of The Public Burning was, one assumes, clear to all in 1977, not least the literary industry: the novel bounced from publisher to publisher amid fears of a notoriously litigious Nixon with nothing better to do in early retirement. The disgraced president’s legacy of détente, Vietnam, the end of the capitalist golden age; all point to the early Cold War as an ideological and economic high tide, if not an outright, and self-evident, turning-point. Where Ragtime hovers “in some new world of past historical time whose relationship to us is problematical indeed,” the one-line synopsis of The Public Burning makes it apparent to the would-be reader that Coover is working with big-H History. Hence “everyday” fictional characters, a criterion established by Georg Lukács for the historical novel, are more or less entirely absent from Coover’s novel. This is achieved partly by a commitment to the theatrical, evidenced by the title and the forms of the intermezzi, and bolstered by the novel’s main divergence from official history—the Rosenberg execution will take place in Times Square.

As Lukács has it, the historical novel, essentially invented as a literary reaction to the French Revolution, is sublated into the realist novel proper, the paragon of which is, naturally, Honoré de Balzac’s Human Comedy. The Revolutionary period (1789-1815) permitted millions of Europeans “to comprehend their own existence as something historically conditioned, for them to see in history something which deeply affects their daily lives and immediately concerns them.” This development is felt not just by the conquering French, but across Europe—Heinrich von Kleist’s Michael Kohlhaas (1810) is surely a historical staging of the persistent backwardness of the nascent German state. For Perry Anderson, the First World War has the exact opposite effect of the French Revolution, delivering a coup de grâce on the already waning form of the historical novel through its sheer meaninglessness, and the Second World War simply “reinforced the effects of the first.” 

Of course, the US barely felt the effects of the First World War; its meaninglessness is usually considered through the battles that preceded American entry into the war: the summer of 1914 revealing the alliance system to be a house of cards, the bloodbath of the Somme in 1916, and so forth. Thus the works that portray the absurdity of the First World War are by and large European. Moreover, the Second World War was felt by its major belligerents as a great conflict between good and evil, and Jameson has elsewhere described it as functioning for Americans as the “moral equivalent of revolution.” One would expect the US, which emerged from the wars greatly strengthened and well and truly within History, and all at far less cost than that of the French revolutionary period, to be the perfect ground for some kind of historicist renaissance. But this was clearly arrested by something, and the prime suspect must be the Cold War.

The first line of The Public Burning proceeds thus: “On June 24, 1950, less than five years after the end of World War II, the Korean War begins, American boys are again sent off in uniforms to die for Liberty, and a few weeks later, two New York City Jews, Julius and Ethel Rosenberg, are arrested by the FBI and charged with having conspired to steal atomic secrets and pass them to the Russians.” Here the Cold War trivialises the Second World War,  revealing the anti-fascist alliance as illusory and the Allied powers’ heroics as nothing more than the ironic prelude to a more properly Manichaean struggle—one constantly reinforced through the rhetoric of the media. Doctorow’s Book of Daniel offers a plangent explanation for this betrayal that is perhaps more psychologically cutting than Coover’s antic formalizations: “That is why we ring our socialist ally who won the war in the East and thereby prevented Fascism from engulfing the West—that is why we ring her borders with military bases. That is what you do to a man who does you a favor. You cannot admit your debt, so you find a way to hate him.”

Coover dramatises this hegemonic struggle through godlike personifications of the superpowers: Uncle Sam, periodically materialising out of thin air to abuse Nixon; and the Phantom, who is constantly referenced but never actually appears. In this Coover is able to resolve the issue of the total absence, in recent history, of “world-historical individuals”: Uncle Sam, with the happy and unwitting help of the media, builds the future of the American system. Uncle Sam is unique in the portrayal of world-historical individuals, however: he is neither the reinforcement of orthodox historical narratives, like Tolstoy’s Napoleon, nor the demystified and legible Robespierres and Cromwells of Hilary Mantel. Instead, he operates as a magnet of revisionism, an explanation for all the sordid acts across the history of the United States—similar to the characterisation in Pynchon’s Inherent Vice of the United States as being literally addicted “to sending kids off to die in jungles.” 

Eric Hobsbawm’s thesis that the apocalyptic rhetoric of the US in the early Cold War was simply an electoral strategy holds good here: Coover’s Uncle Sam is the inverse of Marx’s Napoleon I—one whose original Eighteenth Brumaire perfected the terror by substituting permanent war, not for “permanent revolution,” but permanent reaction. The postmodern emerges in the economic sphere as the shift from capitalist production to capitalist speculation. But insofar as the postmodern is “the becoming economic of the cultural and the becoming cultural of the economic,” we may well detect the emergence of the postmodern in the cultural sphere before we do the economic. The execution of the Rosenbergs was pure spectacle, as evidenced by Uncle Sam’s carnival-barker-like roaring:

“‘Philosophers have explained the world,’ [Uncle Sam] cries, ‘it is necessary to CHANGE the world! So hang on to your hats, folks, cause jist as that old astronomicalizin’ Prophet Nate Ames soothsaid nigh onto two hundred years ago, the Coelestial Light directed here by the Finger of God is gonna drive out the long! long! Night of Heathenish Darkness! I shit you not! stand back! it’s the NEW New Enlightenment!’”

What could be a more suitable inaugural postmodernist moment than this public burning?

by Daniel Horowitz (Reporter at Large)

 

The Graduate Center and the Empire State Building share an intersection. Guy de Maussepant, it is said, lunched in the Eiffel Tower’s cafe regularly. It was the only place, he remarked, where its tasteless erection did not mar the view of his Paris. We are prohibited from replicating this elegant quip by the price of our own tower’s restaurants; or, if not actually the price, by the modest ethos of attending public school. I was commissioned for a piece of field reportage, all travel and lodging expenses paid, by this same principle of thrift: I was sent out the front door. I was sent across Fifth Avenue.

It was a beautiful summer morning in an early autumn that forgot to arrive because a glacier gave up its ghost in a sleepy Finnish suburb and the mob was clotting this same spot, by bus, subway, jet and cab, to see the Empire State Building. They’ve come to the wrong place.

Like Hokusai’s Mount Fuji, the 102-floor monument has been best viewed serrated by clotheslines in the slums of the Lower East Side; or as an apparition through the smog over the tall grass, from the pine barrens across Jersey’s badlands; or amidst the soundtrack of Spanish Harlem’s stoops, competing with a whole park’s worth of sycamores and elms, and winning. On the day of its ribbon cutting, May Day 1931, even its architect sailed three miles out into New York Harbor, away from the ecstatic speeches pronouncing the vertical era, away also from the invisible legal border where Prohibition was in effect. He popped champagne and toasted the skyline, above which hovered his centerpiece. Why gawp at its wide base?

Gazing upwards beside a family of four, I attempted to match their transports of joy. I could not. The brute insensitivity produced by repetition, physical discomfort, and sensory self-preservation left this mythic site, to me, barren. I talked to the streets, to the million visiting Atlases that held up this building’s glory.

“For a school newspaper?” asked a sundazzled Swede, curbed with his family, pausing to assess whether this impromptu interview was the entree to an infamous metropolitan scam he had missed in his guidebook. Deciding it was not, he answered my question. “Yes, to see the Empire State Building of course.”

Another family I spoke to was from Minneapolis. A stunning gentleman consuming two cigarettes was “not interested.” A couple of pensioners from Spain explained: “It’s the symbol of New York. Don’t you feel you are here? I have vertigo already and we haven’t even gone up. Our tickets are not until—when is it, Julian? One.”

Three hours I’d been there witnessing the periapsidal flows of bodies by the busload around the attraction arriving, departing, scattering, going up. The sun hits 34th Street from three angles, reflected off the glass flanks of towers towards the Hudson, a crepuscular trigonometry whose light and heat was reaching just then its crescendo. The Empire State Building is a piecemeal tower whose complete perception is impossible. From outside the Build-A-Bear workshop; from the threshold of “Culture House” on the corner of 35th (which is, despite its nominal titillation, alas a weed shop with a bouncer, painted Smurf blue); from 5th Avenue across the equally promising store, for protein bars at 400% markup, named “ETC.”—the montage of this dismembered monument reflects my gaze to the grubby street.

What strange economy is operating at the base of this skyscraper? What is the sex life of minnows in the shadow of a Great White Shark? Never have I seen a resource more renewable than the pleasure and awe extracted from the Empire State Building; each touristic eye shaving not even a molecule from the limestone of its fame. The opposite: each visitor makes its mythos more mathematically sublime. Tourism, no matter how much an industry, exists around objects entirely removed from exchange: people desire precisely what cannot be bought, a deliverance of the imagination, a waking dream, the bodily fact of “being there.” The industry consists in what are really the penumbras of this free thing, the tertiary infrastructures whose benefits and ravages are famous and debated. This is my dearest hope: that cosmopolitans have travelled this far to seek out the silence of money’s talk; to hear in their heart, wanting wonder not ownership, “Your money is no good here.”

By tourists’ failure to achieve that height, the more stationary inhabitants of the streetside earn livings at the edge of this vortex’s infinite bounty. Pedi-cabbers blasting “Empire State of Mind” competing like peacocks with LED displays; hot dog carts producing redolent steam; Halal carts named not quite after their product but permission in general; folding tables laid with sunglasses, scarves, hats, I ❤ NY memorabilia, and the special repertoire of attire that has somehow become standard, Daddy’s Little Meatball shirts; and Make America Great Again hats sold, with commerce’s deadpan democracy, alongside their parody: Make America Gay Again, Make America Grate. Most prominent are the heirs to the carnival barker pitching tour buses in red outfits. They repeat this chilling jingle: “Tickets sold! Statue of Liberty! Nine Eleven!” The omission of “memorial” —a sympathetic concession to concision—troubled this New Yorker’s heart. I engaged a bus hawker in a brief interview.

“Mostly I just give directions,” he told me, squinting philosophically and sneaking a hit from a sleeved vape. “Yeah, it’s easy to forget it’s everybody’s first time. They know it’s important but, when they get here, they can’t remember why. They want to ride the bus and hear about it. You should talk to an actual tour guide, I mean. You should buy a ticket and hop on.”

Seeing is free, but people pay lavishly for poetry, to gilt the edges of memory’s take-away from the borough’s now-8th tallest skyscraper (and falling). Perhaps the most felicitous rhetorician of this city is memorialized in The Cruise (1998) which documents the thoughts and work of Timothy “Speed” Levitch who speaks into his microphone atop a double-decker Grey-Line passing this spot. “If architecture is the history of all phallic emotion, the Empire State Building is utter catharsis, and we are sitting in its silhouette.” Part of the humor of the film comes from the sly pans to this man’s audience who sit in content multi-lingual incomprehension: they have no idea what Speed is saying; he is bad at his job.

The speculative wealth of late bull market made material, the boom skyscrapers financed from 1924-9 were tombstones of capitalism’s collapsed hopes. They were emblems of plummeting: not only spire-graphs fleeing their peaks but in widespread shots of stockbrokersuicides, in stories of secretaries who, as subordinates of avaricious office managers, were rendered fallen women in the new workplace climate of claustrophobic erotic menace. A sequence of publicity stunts were designed to fill this tower which was scarcely populated until after the Second World War. For two decades, a porter was on staff whose job was to simulate occupation by flipping on the lightswitches of the dozens of empty floors at dusk so the windows glowed with the implication of employment: it was left to his discretion when to send the spectral workers home, finally dimming their offices. The world’s tallest man visited the world’s tallest building; six Clydesdales pulled a carriage filled with kegs of Budweiser to its front door to celebrate the end of Prohibition. Of all promotionals, King Kong (1933) was the most successful. It made the building a global icon and expressed the ambiguity of rise and fall. The racialized Kong was an allegory for the virile multi-ethnic working class who manufactured the city’s symbols (immigrant steelworkers indeed scaled the tower) but were denied its fruit, embodied by the white womanhood of actress Ann Darrow, clutched in the ape’s fist, crammed, as they were, in low-rise ghettos.

It was the massive influx of workers to the site of the Empire State Building’s construction in 1930 that amplified the troubles of the intersection’s predecessor. Benjamin Altman was the first to move his store to 34th Street, in 1906, having come up from Orchard Street’s musty counter trades and again upgrading from 14th Street’s proto-department store row in search of even more respectability after sharing a cross street with prostitution, gambling dens, bars and the Sixth Avenue Elevated. The building he commissioned now houses the Graduate Center. Macy’s would follow soon after, to its current location, the “largest store in the world,” then Gimbels and Ohrbach’s. Eventually competing department stores profused from 6th to 10th Avenues. The problem for Altman’s was this from its opening: the immigrant garment workers that filled the district to the west were mostly housed on the east side of the factories and hung around the borderland of 5th Avenue, between their sweatshops and their homes, scaring away the vital woman shoppers of the middle and upper classes.

Benjamin Altman was a collector of Rembrandts, Hals and Vermeers (his posthumous bequest of the latter was the first Vermeer to enter the MET’s collection) and his taste for chiaroscuro, profusions of texture, and the hypnotism of composition containing seemingly multiple central nodes were evident in his epic window displays that were designed to be visible from even the top tier of a double decker bus, each product an object d’art. Thus, his arrival on 34th was a double scandal. For the working classes, the Roman arches in plateglass both displayed the glistening images of aspiration and acted, also, as physical barriers to their possession: inspiration to feel the devastating disenfranchisement of a totally owned world. For upper classes the scandal was Altman’s dramatic move in the race uptown, intruding into a till-then residential neighborhood whose riches were decidedly private. This was what the WP A Guide of 1939 pinned as his prime influence:

“In order to appease protesting residents, Altman erected a building whose mundane function was decorously hidden by a facade resembling a Florentine palace; until recently not even the owner’s name appeared on the exterior. As commerce—having thus crept in disguise into the avenue—appropriated most of the district, residents moved farther up the avenue.”

In a sense, the innovations of the B. Altman department store would be the incorporation of the commercial and the residential. It was the first to have a cafe inside, not only for the “ladies who lunch” of the leisure classes but for where rising middle class women, from the consuming classes, could safely dine unaccompanied during a respite in their labors. And, perhaps most importantly, it was the first store to contain public restrooms. One could shop all day, and “shopping” could complete its blossoming into an activity, even a vocation, that would resist vehemently the adjective “mundane,” being embedded in aestheticized life.

When, a quarter century later, the monumental office building was to rise across the way and cast its long shadow over Altman’s, it was the apotheosis of these developments, unifying work, leisure and art. Manufacturing’s flight from the immediate neighborhood was foreshadowed by Altman’s own imperial stocking practices: he was also the first to have a dedicated buyer in Paris, a position that soon came to be considered de rigueur for all the city’s stores. His buyers spiraled outwards. A 1931 guidebook to New York informs us,

“Lovely expensive laces, rugs, furniture and tapestries make Altman’s a kind of rare merchandising museum constantly replenished by buyers who travel all over the world and brave war, bandits and pestilence in line of duty. An Altman rug buyer was held up by bandits in Persia and robbed not only of his rugs but his clothes. A lace buyer was three times blown up during the war and once was locked in a military prison. He also sailed the Bay of Biscay when it was a sea of mines and went into Switzerland on a diplomatic passport when the border was closed. That’s what laces mean to Altman’s—and no wonder since customers sometimes order $50,000 worth of them at a time.”

The local garment district began its atrophy during the Second World War. Along with its decades-long decline (that did not hit bottom till the 90s) so went the lofts and slums to the east that had threatened 5th Avenue commerce. The Empire State Building, left behind when the cloud of construction workers dissipated, was a harbinger of the new kind of worker that would dominate the city, also migrating uptown, this time from Wall Street. The office worker, child of the Confuscian bureaucrat and triumph of Monastic life escaped from its rural segregation would be the figure of the century. Even now, the Empire State Building’s anchor tenant is LinkedIn: a company whose work is recursive in the self-propagation of office work. Whereas Altman’s windows were portals to the wide, ownable, world, the Empire State Building’s were designed instead to lay flush with their limestone casing, at great expense of engineering ingenuity, so that its rising shaft read as a monumental unified plane as opposed to a layered conglomerate of individual floors and offices (compare its facade with the Woolworth Building of 1913 whose windows are inlaid and looks like a waffle iron). As Auden writes “In Praise of Limestone”—“The blessed will not care what angle they are regarded from, / Having nothing to hide.” The history of the modern skyscraper has been the refinement of this trick: the unificationof transparency and monument. On this intersection: the world was delivered and then—its people followed.

The sun was beginning to set over New Jersey. Food carts were towed away behind trucks. Vans were loaded with unsold streetside merchandise. The buildings expelled their workers from above ground to under, into subways and happy hours. The last tourists stood in line to take an elevator to the Empire State Building’s observation desk. There is where the building’s pathos is expressed, imposing limits on its gesture of unlimited rise (its silver mast was even intended to be a mooring point for visiting dirigibles, extending its elevator to infinity; but none ever came.) The year after its opening, F. Scott Fitzgerald expressed this paradox:

“Full of vaunting pride the New Yorker had climbed here and seen with dismay what he had never suspected, that the city was not the endless succession of canyons that he had supposed but that it had limits… New York was a city after all and not a universe, the whole shining edifice that he had reared in his imagination came crashing to the ground.”

Witnessing this, then, even the tourist can go home. As I inhabited the street all day, interviewing its denizens and writing this brief report—I, also, was made to understand my place. We do it for the world, living the beautiful myths of what happens in a metropolis. Just how Bohemians learn to rowdily inhabit Left Bank cafes even if there’s not a tourist in site, to furnish their part of the world with a beloved ethos, so the intellectual thinks in New York City. I ascended The Graduate Center to the fourth floor, to retrieve my backpack from the English Department apres a long day of reporting. The Fourth floor? Altman’s Drapery Department, upholstery too; fabrics from afar.

by Aida Eloumri

Get your wallets out, soccer fans, the countdown to the most anticipated tournament of the summer has already started. With only eight months away until kick off,  at the Estadio Azteca in Mexico City on June 11th, 2026, excitement is in the air for fans and teams alike to watch the beautiful game live. A fan myself, I have begun saving so that I might watch the beautiful game on the highest stage at MetLife Stadium. However, due to FIFA’s new pricing mechanism, I (and anyone else of slender means) will potentially be barred by exorbitant fees. 

On Wednesday September 10th, FIFA released the first round of applications for the tournament in partnership with VISA, meaning that eligible VISA cardholders could exclusively apply for tickets until Friday September 19th. However, fans were surprised to find out that FIFA is going to be utilizing “dynamic pricing” for the tournament.  Dynamic pricing is a technique utilized by businesses for maximum flexibility in pricing, allowing for instantaneous increases on goods based on fluctuations in demand. This means that the previous price range,“ $60 for group stage matches to $6,730 for the final,” is subject to change—and for the worse. 

This is an about-face of the method of ticket sales in Qatar, which hosted the tournament in 2022. One of the main perks FIFA got rid of was special resident prices for those who are residents in the US, Canada and Mexico. In prior tournaments, Category 4 tickets were reserved for residents of the host nation (typically at a discounted price). This pales in comparison to the Qatar 2022 World Cup, where they only charged residents $11. Now, the cheapest Category 4 tickets are starting at $60, a 445% increase from three years ago. The reasoning behind this was due to the amount of “purchasing power” Americans had. This assumption (the American dollar is strong and therefore so are those paid its wages)  ignores the dire current economic situation here in the US. I, like many others, was devastated;  we are being actively priced out, and right in our backyard. 

As a soccer fan, it is upsetting to see how FIFA is willing to prioritize profit over the beautiful game. We have seen before how dynamic pricing has caused trouble for fans who have wanted to watch their favorite teams, or to see their favorite artists live. If recent history is any indication—from the Taylor Swift-Ticketmaster chaos during her ERAS Tour (of which I was personally victim) to Inter Miami abusing the technique due to their main-draw Lionel Messi—dynamic pricing is going to price out locals and international fans alike. 

Back in 2022, after waiting over four years since her Reputation Stadium Tour, fans like myself were ecstatic to find out that Taylor Swift was going back on tour, performing old, re-released songs plus new material she had released during the pandemic. I remember vividly when tickets went on sale; my friends and I queued on the Ticketmaster app and were instantly given the runaround—resale tickets starting at $600. I was not the only one who was upset by the organization of the presale. Fans all over the country expressed outrage over how impossible it was to get their hands on tickets. 

Though Swift enjoined Ticketmaster to not utilize dynamic pricing, the company opened the flood gates for bots and scalpers, who promptly sold them on third party platforms (like Ticketmaster) for triple the original price. Ticketmaster has since been sued by the Department of Justice in 2024 over monopolizing ticket sales. Perhaps FIFA should heed their warning. Though it is already perhaps too late, fans are taking aim at the federation online, expressing outrage over dynamic pricing. One fan from England expressed their frustration to ESPN: “ These prices are astonishing — $2,000 for the cheapest final ticket is unacceptable.If fans are successful in obtaining a category four ticket from the first game to the last, that could set them back $3,180 at least. That is more than double what Qatar cost.” And this is not to even mention the expense of US travel during the summer months. To put it otherwise: fans are going to be out a lot of money for a tournament hosted by one of the biggest non-profits in the world. 

After relations between the Qatari-owned Paris St Germain and World Cup champion Lionel Messi collapsed, the four-time UEFA Champions League winner needed to find a new home. Fans speculated a last-dance comeback to F.C Barcelona, where he started his glorious career. Given Barcelona’s shambolic finances, this was an impossibility for one of the world’s most highly paid athletes. Ultimately, after flirting with the sportswashing and cash-flush Saudi League, Messi went to Inter Miami. Soon ecstasy graded to despair as fans saw stadium tickets skyrocket. Prior to Messi’s arrival, tickets often sold for $30; after, prices shot up 500%: tickets for a regular season game became $867 to $2,720 for standard seats.  This sort of financial chicanery is becoming common in world soccer, and since the World Cup has been expanded to 48 teams, it is not out of the question for FIFA to capitalize at every turn: higher prices for certain nations, price-gouging for star-studded line-ups, “dynamic” prices for all possible selling-points. 

We have seen how dynamic pricing has angered fans in the past. From Swifties not being able to see their idol in real life to Inter Miami fans not being able to afford the usurious prices of their money-hungry club, the effects of dynamic pricing are clear. On the local level, Democratic mayoral nominee Zohran Mamdani has recently launched a petition to get FIFA to end dynamic pricing, put a cap on resale tickets,  and set aside 15% of tickets for residents. I call on all fans to mobilize and send a message, telling them to put an end to dynamic pricing for this upcoming tournament. If we believe that the beautiful game is for everyone, we should show it by ending this money-hungry agenda.

By Meg Kaizu

 “A Century of The New Yorker” runs through February 21, 2026 at the Stephen A. Schwarzman Building. “Magazine Fever: Gen X Asian American Periodicals” ran through August 31st.

The New York Public Library’s exhibition “A Century of The New Yorker” draws on the Library’s collections, including the magazine’s archives and the papers of many of its contributors, to reflect on the stories and ideas that created the New York’s most bien pensant magazine. Since 1925, The New Yorker has cultivated a sensibility both rarefied and aspirational, appealing to the about-town and upwardly-mobile citizens of what once was called “the capital of the world.” The magazine was shaped by the founding vision of Harold Ross and Jane Grant and built upon by generations of staff, setting expectations for singular style, socially engaging writing, journalistic rigor, and unique art, with a dash of snootiness.

The story of The New Yorker, including the brilliant talents and imperfect media workers who created the magazine, has been told in the pages of over 5,000 issues that have gone to print in its first 100 years. But a more profound history may be explored in the magazine’s archives of the collections of The New York Public Library, which comprises the exhibition (hosted in the Rayner Special Collections Wing of the Stephen A. Schwartzman building). Through correspondence, manuscripts, memos, artifacts and artworks, the exhibition chronicles the complex stories of editorial relationships, diligent typists and fact-checkers and talented artists, as well as the social and political changes in the US.

In ways that are visible and invisible, The New Yorker has shaped the public’s understanding of various aspects of the world, touching on such intricate subjects as war and violence, race and gender, the environmental movement, and the distinctiveness of American fiction writing. The exhibition examines how the magazine has featured John Hersey’s long-form essay about the atomic bombing of Hiroshima in the August 31, 1946 issue. The exhibition displays a copy of the issue with a caption explaining how John Hersey’s seminal 1946 New Yorker piece was a turning point in the course of investigative journalism in the US. Hersey was a war correspondent in the Pacific and became one of the first American journalists to visit Hiroshima after the US detonated an atomic bomb on the city on August 6, 1945. Harsey began collecting eyewitness accounts for a New Yorker story, which became a detailed 30,000-word piece tracing the experience of six survivors. His piece explored the human and ethical ramifications of the atomic age.  Two months before its publication, Hersey proposed that the piece be printed and published in four parts. Instead of publishing it in installments, however, William Shawn convinced Harold Ross to devote an entire issue to Hersey’s historic report, which was a first for the magazine. The magazine cover features Charles E. Martin’s illustration depicting people going about their lives, enjoying activities like sports, bicycling, yardwork, dancing, reading in an idyllic urban environment with trees and a river. The display still has a strip of white paper enfolding the magazine, with a line that reads: “This entire issue is devoted to the story of how an atomic bomb destroyed a city.” At the time of distribution, the thin strip of paper functioned to alert its readers to the sensitivity of the content.

Apart from Hersey’s 1946 piece, another featured issue is entitled “Illustrating the Enemy” (The New Yorker, October 31, 1942). The caption describes how, in 1942, less than a year after the United States entered WWII, Rea Irvin created an illustration of Adolf Hitler as a witch perched on a broomstick for the New Yorker’s Halloween cover. Ross generally avoided publishing cover art depicting public figures but this illustration by Irvin was a rare exception. The caption explains that Irvin caricatured another Axis Power Japan, drawing the three jack-o’-lanterns to the left side of the cover with stereotypical Asian features. The caption explains that in the wake of the Pearl Harbor bombing, “racist caricatures” of the Japanese allowed white America to “other” their enemy and soon after this depiction served as a justification for imprisoning thousands of Japanese Americans in U.S. internment camps.  

The NYPL exhibition examines how the artworks and writings of The New Yorker reflected and, in some cases, reinforced the biases readers and the public held and how domestic and international news was curated to sway public opinion. The exhibition offers an opportunity for us to reflect on how we may view ethnic and racial minorities and foreigners and how images on paper, or on TV, may influence our perception in the present moment. In its contributors and its content, The New Yorker has reflected both the lofty ideals and the historically rooted inequalities, which arguably defines the American experience in ways that continue to shape our societal views and political landscape in the 21st Century.

The Museum of Chinese in America’s “Magazine Fever: Gen X Asian American Periodicals” traces the history of Asian American magazines in the US, exploring the impact the periodicals had on not only Asian America but also broader American society. The exhibition illuminates how Asian American magazines have reflected the new consciousness and energy of the American post-war. In the late 1960s and early 1970s, the Asian American Movement agitated for anti-colonial Third World solidarity, and the establishment of ethnic studies programs in universities. Printed materials became instrumental for the movement at that time. The first issue of Cidra, a newspaper founded by Japanese American students at UCLA, conveyed the cut of the new jib of the new identity, rejecting the passive Oriental stereotype, signifying the birth of a new Asian American. The publications of this era provided spaces for cultural creativity and art, paving ways for a new visual and literary expression for Asian Americans. Original copies of Cidra from 1969 and 1970 are exhibited, alongside other publications such as Yellow Seeds and Asian Americans for Action. The periodicals from this era embodied the new potency and the shifting political landscape, sometimes featuring articles bilingually. The issue of Cidra in the image is from March 1970. 

In the 1980s and 1990s, Asian American identity transformed from a vision coming out of political agitation into a broadly recognized demographic. Through periodical publishing, which was a vital form of mass media in the 1990s, Asian American media workers editorialized issues that were crucial to their communities, daring to depict Asian Americans in ways previously unimaginable. The exhibition presents stories of Generation X magazines—how they were founded and operated and how they captured the ethos of multiculturalism and Generation X ideas such as defiance and intersectionality. Moreover, it offers a space to reflect on how these periodicals influenced the ways in which Asian American identity may be understood today. Drawn from MOCA’s Private Danny Chen Collection and Archives, the exhibition showcases the Asian American magazine publishing during the multicultural era, including A. Magazine, AsiAm, AsianWeek, Audrey, Giant Robot, Hyphen, Jade, KoreAm, Rice, Transpacific, Yolk, and others.

Founded in 1979, AsianWeek had chronicled the growing presence, prominence and influence of Asian Americans in politics and culture in the US, until its closure in 2009. As an English language magazine, AsianWeek was geared towards readers who didn’t speak languages that their immigrant parents and grandparents spoke. Distributed by mail to a subscriber base numbered at its height over 50,000 nationally, the magazine provided analysis of local and national election cycles, interpretations of census data, immigration news, and international news coverage of historic events such as the Hong Kong handover to China in 1997. It also provided a critical space for opinionated commentary from emerging Asian American pundits. The headlines such as “Asian American income tops them all” and “Making the Grade” convey the aspirational and integrationist concerns of Asian Americans at the approach of the millennium.  

The exhibition also touches on issues of multiculturalism, which was the dominant racial framework and discourse of the 1980s and 1990s. The exhibition expands on what multiculturalism was trying to achieve, explaining that on one level, multiculturalism was a rejection of the assimilationist ideal of a melting pot society, where all minority cultures are integrated into a monoculture. It was also a celebration of America’s diversity. At the same time, the exhibition explains that the politics of difference that attended multiculturalism made some cultural workers uneasy. The exhibition invites visitors to wonder about multiculturalism’s impact on the broader American society, cultural shift, and how this has affected Asian American experience.  

A.Magazine was created in 1989 and was published bi-monthly, to trace “the emerging outlines of Asian America,” according to one of the founders Jeff Yang. For 12 years until its closure in 2002, the magazine was an outlet of Asian American cultural reportage, editorials and entertainment features targeted to a young, educated readership of second-generation children of immigrants. It had a national subscription base and was sold in major newsstands like Barnes and Noble and Borders Books. It was known to be the prominent media platform for Asian American life through the 1990s, with the professional editorial staff and emerging cohort of gifted writers. Many celebrities of the decade graced its covers such as Jenny Shimizu, presenting an image of defiant Asian beauty and power. Viewed in the context of multiculturalism, this style may be understood to rebuke the idea that Asian Americans should melt into assimilation. Visitors can view several copies of the magazine that expressed the vigor and style of this era on its glossy covers.

As a response to the closing of A.Magazine, Hyphen was created in 2002. It was founded and run by Asian American women, a rare occurrence in the history of Asian American periodicals. Hyphen sought to counter uncritical celebrations of Asian American success and stereotypes of Asians as math geeks and perpetual foreigners. Its editorial vision mixed hard-hitting journalism and off-beat cultural coverage, with unique artworks, and the magazine’s name indicated “intersectionality of identity” and “hyphens as connectors.” Hyphen, as was the case with many other magazines featured in the exhibition, closed in the mid-2010s. Hyphen’s covers in the gallery reveal the editors’ intentions to create images of Asian Americans that were different from the earlier publications. The exhibition chronicles the history of Asian American magazine publishing, highlighting the shifting landscape of politics and media and cultural industries of the past several decades in the US. While it has an elegiac tone in its examination of the past, the exhibit also deftly indicates how this history is relevant for understanding issues of the present. 

In closing, I would like to invoke Alison Butler’s concept of “binarism” — a discursive and linguistic motif with the logics of self and other at work, specifically, in relation to race and gender in her book “Women’s Cinema.” Butler introduces Hamid Naficy’s “accented cinema” to avoid vague “melting pot rhetoric” and her examples of “binarism” include the margins defined in relation to the mainstream and the feminine existing only in relation to the masculine . In explaining these issues, Butler discusses several women filmmakers whose works explore formal patterns other than binarism. Butler addresses the danger that exists beyond the exilic community from which images and ideas emerge and address issues in the first instance, while the binary patterning may invite readings and interpretations, such as exoticism or demonization of the other. These instances ambiguate image-making and storytelling. Through the process of globalization, the politics of location and dislocation are “complicated by the possibility that translational and transcultural reception may revise or even reverse the meanings of artworks.” While looking at the two exhibitions, I felt a sense of ambivalence, thinking of the emerging digital and virtual worlds, reflecting on the magazine publishing of the past several decades.

By Michael Villanova

Here is a list of things that Eddington, Ari Aster’s 2025 film, is not about. It is not a mirror of pandemic life that merely shows us the confusion and loneliness of a tumultuous period, a period in which everyone – regardless of political ideology – was affected by. It is not a piece of snide centrism that tells us everyone is at blame, a saccharine pox on both houses that wants us to yearn for a world without conflict or violence. It is not a schmaltzy lament on “how we got here” that finger wags to the audience about having to act kinder towards one another.  

Set during the lead up to a Mayoral election in a small town outside of Albuquerque during the early days of the COVID-19 pandemic, Eddington is a film about a person who wishes that things will fall apart. More intent on capturing moods and the feelings of the pandemic, the film pits Sherriff Cross (Joaquin Pheonix) against the town’s Mayor Ted Garcia (Pedro Pascal) over COVID restrictions, what is right and wrong, and, ultimately, who is a better person. Over the course of the film, we see Cross develop from a man who is most content with simply being there to someone whose dreams and fantasies produce a world where the misery, loneliness, and confusion that he experiences are part of a grand conspiracy.  

The characters of Eddington, it would appear, are enveloped in real conspiracies as much as they are also driven by online conspiracies. It is true that the liberal elite, personified in Mayor Garcia, are selling out the town and in the final scenes accomplish their globalist plot, as it were, with the help of a Native tribe by setting up a huge resource-draining data processing plant for an AI company. (Aster has remarked that that the mediation we experience by phones and algorithms – the triumph of which is represented in the building of the data processing plant – is what Eddington is about). It is true that ANTIFA supersoldiers are being paid by some shadowy cabal to ruin small towns, flown in on a private jet. And because of Cross’ anger, it is true that whoever murdered Mayor Garcia is indeed covering it up.  

In light of the many real conspiracies going on, the conspiracies rattled off inside Sherriff Cross’ home by his caustic mother-in-law, Dawn (Deirdre O’Connell) and anxious wife, Louise (Emma Stone) are not fantastical flights from reality per se. Over the course of the film, the two of them eagerly consume and speculate on various conspiracies they read online. As we find out, the specter of the father-in-law, the former Sherriff of Eddington and of whom a shrine has been erected in Sherriff Cross’ house, looms over why Dawn and Louise are attracted to conspiracies. For Louise, her newfound belief that there are pedophile cults that are abducting children, raping them, and then warping their memories so that they forget about their abuse stems from her own experience being raped by her well-respected father and hiding her abortion. The mother’s conspiracizing comes from wanting to remain ignorant of this all too obvious fact. The pedophiles are not in her house: they’re controlling the world and spreading viruses to wrought pain on the world. Displacement for the daughter or repression for the mother, conspiracizing is not just a way of making sense of things but a way of holding onto things, preserving world, and coming out stronger from never ending tumult. As it turns out, Dawn’s hunch that her son-in-law did not do enough to save her husband’s life is confirmed in a way she could not even predict. Let the world fall apart: with a conspiracy in hand, one can come out unscathed, proven right, or on top.
