The monotony of Eddington’s first two acts is juxtaposed against these multiple conspiracies. The everydayness that Aster presents could be mistaken for “realism” or an attempt to portray pandemic life accurately (although, it does in fact pull from several real incidents or conspiracy theories). Aster’s capacity to capture certain character types like the crypto obsessed Sherriff Michael or Sarah, the young white activist ready to police other people’s behavior, are all too perfect renderings of types born of the past decade. And as much as it seems that puerile activists organize the BLM protests in Eddington, they are at least, in some sense, sincere: awkward in their approach and reasons for protesting but nonetheless trying to speak out against a real injustice. But as a film that largely centers on Sherriff Cross and the world he inhabits, Aster spends more time exposing the mediocrity of an all-too-common person today. The person who believes in paranoid delusions of immigrant gangs and white replacement might be politically extreme, but he is also extremely average. Or an average person could easily become a Sherriff Cross. The lack of inner life that the film offers about Cross highlights how normal a person like Cross is today: a person who is quietly aware of their timidity and shallowness but finds strength when lashing out. Such a person is both unexceptional but silently believes they are primed for greatness. 

Each one of Sherriff Cross’ fantasies – personal or political – legitimizes his simmering anger and violence. The BLM protestors that crop up in his town do not really know why they are protesting and therefore their protests are unserious (in fact, one such young protestor will become a Kyle Rittenhouse conservative influencer when everything pans out); there really are paid outsiders who are coming to destroy your small down; the drifter in your town really is a menace to the peace; and your wife will leave you despite the fact that you are a decent guy. The latter figure, the scorned divorced middle-aged man, has become something of an internet meme: if there is an angry middle-aged man recording a rambling video in their car chances are they are either divorced, their kids no longer want to talk to them, or both. But like manosphere influencers, Sherriff Cross is someone who wants to be important. In his final showdown with Mayor Garcia, Sherriff Cross goes to Garcia’s house to address a noise complaint. Entering a masked, socially distanced fundraiser party with Katy Perry’s bromide charged “Firework” playing in the background, Cross tries to quite the blasting music. Garcia simply turns the music back on, slaps Cross twice (Cross had, the night before, accused Garcia of committing statutory rape with his wife years ago), and then Cross silently walks out. 

Yet, between Cross’ accusation against Garcia and Cross impotently walking out of a party to a pop anthem, there is a short but important scene. Cross wakes up in the middle of the night to take a swig of water and, like so many of us, goes to mindlessly scroll on his phone. In his hypnagogic state, he feeds his mind more images of violence and of anti-immigrant memes: more things to be afraid of. He falls back asleep and awakes to find that his wife has posted a video stating that, as a child, she was raped by her father and has decided to run off with a charismatic right-wing new age leader.  

What follows is Sherriff Cross’ justified revenge, the necessary violence to expose and end the evil in the world. We can read the end of the movie as something akin to a fantasy sequence: finally, Sherriff Cross matters. He can finally be the cowboy. In the movie’s climatic long closing action sequence, everything is elevated to a ridiculous sense of proportion with huge explosions, a fire spelling out “NO PEACE” in the desert orchestrated by ANTIFA, and epic gun fights between Cross and those peace-hating anarchists. Cross’ conspiratorial dreams have come true!  

In the movie’s most breathtaking sequence, Cross falls down the side of a hill during his ANTIFA shootout. His descent is akin to the buffalo on the movie’s David Wojnarowicz poster. If Wojnarowicz’s Untitled (Buffalo) depicts a country confidently in decline, a country that steadfastly charges unto its death as it ignores or even celebrates the mass deaths of the AIDS pandemic, Sherriff Cross’s descent down the hill is a self-imposed parody of this decline. Gaining his footing, he makes his way onto the roof of a local history museum and falls through. As if mocking the fact that this film passes for a modern-day Western, Cross picks himself up from the rubble of (probably fake) Native artifacts, mannequins of Native people, and dioramas of life in the old West. But amongst the rubble of the museum Sherriff Cross emerges as a simulacrum like other right-wing men today: crude imitations of a past that they yearn for, that they want to embody but, wracked with anxiety and paranoia, are unable to. As he rushes out of the museum, we do not see the disheveled and asthmatic Cross as one of the men he might idealize in the old west. He is not some tough guy civilizing an untamed world. But the fantasy sequence allows him to be a very tough guy, killing ANTIFA supersoldiers if just for a few minutes and making the conspiracizing and destruction of the town he defends all worth it. (Eddington finds affinity with Kiyoshi Kurosawa’s recent film Cloud that had an American release at the same time as Aster’s film. Kurosawa’s film follows a young online reseller who rips people off in pursuit of living a seemingly average life. When the people he rips off come together to kill him, the reseller and his victims are quickly shown to be idiotic imitators of real gangsters who can successfully execute and deal with the violence that comes with the territory of a criminal enterprise. Both movies depict two middling and shallow men unequipped to navigate a world they think they should master). 

Eddington is a movie almost designed to make a certain type of viewer desire that some character will come on screen at the end and say, “this is all terrible, Trumpism is the cause of this.” But the lack of such a pronouncement is not an endorsement of Sherriff Cross by Aster. Nor, do I think, is it an ask on behalf of the viewer to empathize with Cross or cry for his suffering. As Cross is stabbed in the head during his ANTIFA standoff, one of the children of Eddington who previously joined BLM protests to impress another activist shoots the final ANTIFA member. In this epilogue, the child becomes a Kyle Rittenhouse-esque cause célèbre, hosting podcasts and posting on TikTok. Cross becomes Mayor of the town he risked everything to save, but he is permanently paralyzed and needs round the clock care; he has become a puppet for his mother-in-law who is calling the shots. One way to read Cross’ fate is that all of this – losing your wife, losing your mobility, losing your dignity – was all worth it. It’s not ideal, but the violence, in the face of such a terrible, no-good world, is necessary. Left unable to speak and paralyzed, there is no way for Cross to gesture this to other characters or the audience. While no one will remember the organizers of the leaderless BLM protests of 2020, the right-wing has recently produced several martyrs and echo chamber influencers, short-lived and mainstays alike, that have grifted their way to the (relative) top and have had their grievances and resentments valorized several times over.  

But such a politics is also awash with people who have ruined their lives and ruined them in the pursuit of preserving their conspiratorial and deluded dreams. Sometimes you come up a Rittenhouse, other times you end up moribund. In saving Eddington, Cross, like many right-wing men, yearn for the chance to prove themselves through gratuitous violence. Thus, unlike Alex Garland’s recent milquetoast intervention on the political moment Civil War, Aster provides us with a glimpse of the all too unexceptional person who fantasizes about violence, who fantasizes about violence because they think they are better humans than everyone else, who fantasizes about violence because they know deep down that their opponents are really just saying left-wing sentiments to get laid, and so on. The tedium of the film, its overinsistence about how Cross’ silly impotence drives his everday life may leave some wanting a different pacing or a different film altogether. Yet, that should not reflect poorly, I suspect, on the film itself but, perhaps, the juncture it dilates and prods at. 

Eddington is deeply joyless; while comedic in its rendering of several personality types, there is little reprieve from the tension of things falling apart. One might even go so far as to say the film, for long stretches, does not even attempt to be interesting. That is to say that contrary to the idea that this is a film that merely seeks to document the pandemic or paint a realistic portrait of when things went really haywire in 2020 – and therefore should be measured for how accurately it is able to reproduce that history – it is a film that brutally delivers the life and feelings of a man that is all too familiar and all too typical today. Such a man may not be exciting or a figure we should root for (despite him feeling that he is victimized and unfairly put upon) but, that little big man, he is everywhere. In capturing a persistent ubiquity, Eddington’s achievement comes from strikingly capturing the exemplary bore of our catastrophic moment.

By Dana Burns

Last year, a local comedian named William Banks stood on a Gowanus stage and announced that, in a few days, he would be beginning an 8-month prison sentence. His crime? Vandalizing some pro-Israel yard signs in a Connecticut suburb. It seemed excessive but, in the era of McCarthyist crackdowns on campuses, plausible. After the show he hawked shirts with his mugshot on it. Then he went offline. 

Some weeks later, grainy cellphone videos started cropping up on his instagram. At first they seemed to show disturbing snippets of harassment in prison. Soon they became irreverent exchanges between him and his cellmate. Then he began reprising a pre-incarceration bit: Banks as a polytheistic cult figure intent on mass conversion. Ostensibly, he had gotten a hold of a flip phone and was smuggling media to the outside world. The videos escalated until he broke out of jail, bought a gun, and started life on the lam. 

It was fully and unequivocally fake, as was eventually revealed. A rouse. A bit. Further proof of the intersection between alt comedy and conceptual art. But also an attempt at making something that – at least at first – felt really, really real. That was the whole point. From the grainy video quality, truncated durations, and untrained actors, the project took pains to approximate some reality of incarcerated life. And the gravity of the situation – some guy’s life getting messed up because of an inane political stunt – along with the realities of prison banality and violence – landed like a truth needing deference. 

Curious, I went to his celebratory “release party” at El Sabor cafe by Myrtle-Broadway, Brooklyn. The last time I’d seen him, in Gowanus, the crowd has been modestly sized, full of staid, careerist media millennials. But the stunt had come with a wave of notoriety; The reels were algorithm-friendly, and spoke to a post-adult swim, Gen Z sensibility. A number of mainstream press write-ups attest to the success of the stunt. The crowd at El Sabor attested to the new paradigm: streetwear kids flooded out into the street. Numerous bouncers guarded the door (and let me in for free when I whispered the code, “I believe in God”). Inside, music was blaring and a makeshift bar was pouring liquor into plastic cups. Banks and his roommates, comedian Will Duncan and Peter McIndoe, stood on a stage that towered over the rest of the audience, flanked by a DJ and entourage. They weren’t performing anything but themselves, loudly occupying the stage as if to energize the crowded, slippery room’s collective jouissance. There was a simmering, agitated atmosphere among the throng of stoners and girls with fake IDs, and I left after 10 minutes.

 

There’s an ambiguity to Banks’ project that the wrap up party failed to answer. What, exactly, is the joke? Is it how far he was willing to go? Is it the actual content of his sketches? Is it that we believed him? 

None of it was exactly funny, but maybe the point wasn’t being funny, per se, but effacing all the cliches of comedy. Emerging from the Tim Heidecker universe, a big part of today’s comedy relies on never quite knowing where the joke ends and who’s in on it. It is as if the pretense of ‘comedy,’ the ‘sketch,’ the artistic persona, now seem innately suspect, as if any overly-defined onset of artifice dulls us into antiquated neural pathways. Paradoxically, Banks’ baroque subterfuge is then a means to some new frontier of authenticity.

The hammer-to-the-frame approach is reminiscent of the avant garde art movements of the past century, and I wondered if there wasn’t some overlap happening. It has been said that alt comedy has become perhaps the most viable creative scene in New York, far outpacing music (a death that Spotify helped usher) and non-institutional arts (even the self-appointed vanguard is allegedly funded by Peter Theil). If this is true, it would make sense that comedy would shoulder the bulk of the creative weight, and maybe even osmose some of its high-brow, arty accreditation in the process. Irony has long been a tool of performance artists – maybe Banks is more their genealogy than “what’s the deal with airplane food?” 

Likely it’s the dearth of humor and abundance of tension that makes Banks seem more Abromović than Hedberg. Banks’ project leans on endurance over artistry, self-refrentiality over story. But years after performance artists broke creative ground, and in an era of influencers and content churning, the selfiness of the stunts lands differently.

 

Ostensibly, the joke isn’t the success of his subterfuge or the content of his prison sketches – it’s being the guy who was pretending to be incarcerated. This is clear in the blurring it takes on between the bit and Banks’ real life. Banks really was arrested over a year ago for vandalizing pro-Israel yard signs – he just wasn’t incarcerated. After Banks began his fictional sentence, he dropped out of his normal life, got dumped by his girlfriend, and went into hiding at a friend’s place outside of NYC. And, since the purported conclusion of his project, he’s only doubled down on the gun-loving, sex-crazed ex-con persona. The jail time might be fake, but it seems that a sense of persecution is a psychic reality for Banks.

The true draw of Banks’ project is that it grants us initiation into a structure of feeling. He is inviting his audience to participate in the construction of himself, and it is in our power to reject or legitimate the person he claims to be, and the reality he claims to experience. In return, we get jouissance by proxy: how far can our attention get this guy to go? How much will he become his character? Does truth actually matter at all at this point? The character Banks has fleshed out is one more at home in the disconcerting milieu of January 6, but the blur between performance and reality emboldens us to feel with the antihero he posits. There’s a problem here that’s moral in nature – do we need to keep emboldening the personalities of angrily dissatisfied white men – but for now let’s focus on where the form goes wrong.

William Banks

While it looks something like performance, Banks’ project functions more as a meme. It derives its humor from repetition, from its spread, and with each new viewer, Banks’ character is instantiated. This is most apparent with the image that came to emblematize the whole project (and emblazon t-shirts): Banks’ actual mugshot. It shows Banks with a blank gaze and wild, thinning hair, looking closer to Ted Kazinsky’s and Timothy McVeigh’s than young Brooklyn comics striving to write for SNL. Not quite a hardened criminal, but a man on the fringes. Like a meme, the image is all potential – the idea of an event – vying to be charismatic enough to actualize.

It’s notable that genes, the original memes, aren’t whole organisms themselves – just one of an organism’s constitutive parts. It needs to be realized as part of something greater than itself in order to actually mean anything. Once upon a time that meant something going viral by dint of its particular charm and the whims of the moment, or it meant Occupy-style anonymity, gaining a cultural upper-hand. But as Banks’ project suggests, there’s a way to skip all the contingencies and speak through the overdetermined form of memeness itself. 

The problem, however, is that there is something deeply self-conscious in this kind of humor. The blurring between what’s real and what’s fake, between real life and the bit, obscures the pretense: that he’s doing comedy, performing a bit. The suggestion is a greater authenticity. SNL needs costumes and scripts and camera crews to be funny, while all the meme needs is to be repeated. Whereas the overdetermined form of the sketch eschews the frame in order to home in on content, Banks’ mimetic stunt simply uses its content to continually bolster its frame. But this also incurs, on the part of Banks, an even more damning problem: while one can create an image, they cannot fabricate a meme. The ostensible spontaneity of the meme contradicts authorship – so how can he lay claim to his own stunt, his own comedic persona, without blowing up its whole pretense?

 

And as for the moral problem. Alt right comedian Sam Hyde provides an instructive example. Whenever a mass shooting occurs, fans share a picture of Hyde holding an automatic rifle, claiming it to be the shooter in question. Sometimes journalists erroneously take up the provocation and publish the photo as fact. While this sounds like a great way to fuck with a public figure, Hyde is in on the bit. It’s not just free publicity, but the comedy itself. It’s how Hyde wants to be seen – contrarian, nihilistic, perhaps dangerous, but also, above all, authentically disengaged. Hyde set up the domino and let the joke play out with the populist horizontalism of a meme.

Sam Hyde

As Hyde’s case shows, there can be something exculpating about the horizontalism of the meme. By abdicating oneself as the author of the meme, one installs a safeguard against criticisms on the level of content. While it might refer to a certain person, a meme always belongs to an impersonal procession of participants. Whereas the persona has always had an unwieldy quality, giving license to say or do things prohibited in everyday life, it was at least linked to an individual. But if a comedian’s function is just offering themself up to the will of the public, isn’t that just to offer me a mirror, reflecting back to me my loudest desires? From the vacuous potentiality of the mugshot meme to the manufactured jouissance of the wrap-up party, Banks wasn’t so much giving us a bit as he was offering up his body like a sacrifice to the share button. As we have seen with the internet writ large, this is a cynical feedback loop – one that starts with an idea but all too often contorts into a painful, destructive writhing towards freedom. 

The role of the entertainer, the artist, the musician, is always in part sacrificial: they offer up their body, their subjectivity, in return for an audience (the money, the love, the sex, the immortalization). For the comedian to offer themself up through meme isn’t all bad, even if it’s a bit lazy. But the thing about a meme like Banks, and unlike a sketch or a film or stand up, is that its whole premise is an unwieldy, diffuse, and semi-obfuscated form of manipulation – a kind of large scale ‘made you look.’ And when we look, and keep looking, we all sign up to manipulate reality together, to trade our ground for the vague feeling of an event, of something happening. Circulating like a miasma around this structure of feeling is an implacable cruelty: the body offered up is rancid, and we eat it like a fast food dinner. We laugh because we were fooled and because they were lying, because jail exists and guns exist and maybe deep down there’s something compelling about angry white guys fucking and preaching. Art is the manufacture of attention. Enjoyment is an endurance test of mimetic deferral. Call me old-fashioned, but I think we might have lost the plot. Sure, we can break the frame – I just don’t think it’s only raw, undulating spectacle waiting for us underneath.

 

 

Postscript:

 

Problematizing the argument a bit, perhaps, is the very material fact that a William Banks memecoin netted tens of thousands of (crypto) dollars for Palestinian aid. The memecoin suggests the attention economy, so to speak, can be charitable as well. The real gains here are admirable, and it’s not for me to denigrate a fundraising method that works. Suffice it to say that one does not cancel out the other: the sticky pointlessness of the meme posits void where there might be craft, while at the same time, its voracious suck can capture the good ends of attention. Where they meet isn’t neutrality; it’s more like the non-existence of Banks points right back to the populace in all its complexity.

My trans friend Riley is getting married next month to a German citizen. She didn’t get her new passport updated to her “living” gender before the Trump Administration started attacking trans people. So, traveling next month she has to navigate flight check-in,TSA agents and law enforcement officers amidst the administration’s increasingly anti-trans rhetoric. Riley, in a text message, told me that getting to Germany now means “doing my best to pretend to be a cis man,” using her “deadname and male ‘gender’ so they don’t give me a hard time.” 

Supposedly heterosexual, cisgendered people live in a society that largely assumes their sexuality is the natural order of things. An institutionalized heterosexism tends to “prefer” people who look and act straight which is “normal,” expected, and advantageous. It confers unearned, often unconscious or taken-for-granted benefits that accrue to supposedly straight people. If you are a sexual minority in this society, most, globally speaking, will choose to conceal this alignment to avoid prejudice and discrimination. 

Culturally-prescribed gender norms, how men and women are celebrated, varies from culture to culture. If your birth-assigned gender matches this society’s universal prescriptions––you are “clockable” as a man or woman in this society––you occupy a privileged position within its gender orthodoxy. Matching the cultural expectations of a man or woman means you are systematically afforded dominance within institutional processes. An entire society with a gender hierarchy like this can be blind to the multiple, omnipresent contradictions to gender norms. It is barely able to, or perhaps just beginning to, see, a continual queerness woven into the human and natural world. Below are four consequences to queer life where a cis-hetero majoritary enforces itself, violently sometimes, on people who, for lots of reasons, do not hide their queer identity in the public sphere. LGBTQ people encounter 3 “types” of social aversion or heterosexism as popular prejudice directed towards them, that has existential consequences on queer life. An insidious heteronormativity that leaves heterosexuality unmarked, bleeds into all four consequences and lives in both straight and queer people. Only a straight and queer “ally of queer” has the power to create more equality for queers.    

This gender orthodoxy will make most queers, unlike straight people, fear anti-queer discrimination. Being out and proud is critical, but it also represents a form of self sacrifice within a system that polices gender norms that produce oftentimes terrorizing outcomes for queer people. It should not be a surprise that even highly progressive Western societies can bring about and authorize an influential group of homo or trans-phobic people––the first consequence to queer life. These are the people with the strongest prejudices towards made-up gender nonconformity, which is seen as a societal threat. In their view, queers are willfully causing an “unnatural” breakdown of “everyday life, family and the economy” as put forward in Judith Lorber and Susan Farrel’s seminal book, The Social Construction of Gender. Their chronic impulse is to censor, harass or otherwise erase queer people at every turn. This parasitically influential group is the most direct threat to what Dr. Patricia Kaishan calls ordinary queer life. 

Homo/trans-phobic political rhetoric and actions, imbued unsurprisingly with a self-righteousness, is sanctioned by multiple religious, cultural and psychological bases. Its rhetoric can conjure and reinstate mainstream anti-LGBTQ anxieties and hence antipathies towards queerness. Trump’s inaugural address sanctimoniously declaring there are only two genders, and, earlier, Ron De Santis’ notorious “Don’t Say Gay” bill in Florida, are just two well-known examples. The Florida bill, flouting the “fundamental right” of parents to choose whether their child is, ominously, “exposed” to LGBTQ content––as opposed to children learning about queerness as imbued in the human experience––is explicitly homophobic. Importantly, the bill’s tropes, now more than ever under the cloak of religious freedom, can effectively reinforce a straight-majoritarian moral superiority with its epistemic upper hand. With the ready potential to whip up a violent surveillance state, the traditional playbook for getting rid of queerness by this group is to leverage this moral authority and make “the freedom to be public, to just be who we are,” “always in contention” as stated in The Queer Nation Manifesto. Trans and bi-phobia can also be quietly enforced in the LGBTQ community. 

The next consequence to queer life are those who are “tolerant” of it. This group may fall short of explicit homo/trans-phobia, but are largely incurious about and unfamiliar with queerness. Their form of aversion manifests in their discomfort around LGBTQ individuals. They likely don’t have any as friends and the result is the tolerant group does not know how queers experience marginalization (it is well understood that a straight person with queer friends is more accepting of them). But the tolerant’s ignorant stance on LGBTQ will rely almost entirely on their own, conceited sense that the government, wrote Kristen Soltis-Anderson about Republican support for LGBTQ, “should not be in the business of meddling with or punishing people because they are gay or lesbian.” Agreeable-sounding enough. But within a self-reinforcing heterosexist social order, I can usually tell I’m talking to someone who is tolerant of me, a distant cousin at a family gathering perhaps, who, if my same sex spouse comes up for some reason, I observe a tense silence. Psychologist Deborah Davis, Ph.D. in an interview described the particulars of these “awkward” interactions as products of a queer person’s own personal experience of being “criticized, shunned or attacked enough times before” for their identity, and particularly “if [they] have unhealed trauma related to such incidents” which can make a queer person hypersensitive and easily triggered. She said that “when you are in the presence of someone who is merely tolerating you, you can sense their tension as you, in turn, become tense. You brace yourself. Are they hostile? Or are they navigating this unfamiliar terrain with you?”

A prevailing heterosexism produces this uncertainty for the queer person in the first place. But  the tolerant person in an authoritative position in this society can insist on their forbearance. Dr. Davis adds their “ruling spirit of acceptance and live-and-let-live” is not enough to create true equality where the tolerant, largely ignorant of queer people’s “emotional, social, and legal struggles” continues to other queers and facilitates them getting “caught up in our differences rather than meeting each other on common ground.” A society that sanctions this detached, self-absorbed sense of fairness can make the tolerant unable to register the recent political tides turning dangerously against queers.  

The third consequence to queer life I’ll call the “gay friendly.” These are the majority of  supposedly straight people who probably have openly gay and lesbian friends—trans and bisexuals, not so much. Greater familiarity with gay people, not surprisingly, means greater comfort and empathy. I can make explicit gay jokes with my gay friendly friends, and they will often freely initiate them. There are even gay friendly Republicans, Soltis-Anderson reports, who “support same sex couples living and thriving side-by-side with heterosexual couples”. 

So far so good. But, when you occupy the preferred, supposedly straight group, the “normative baseline” says Danielle Kie Hart, the gay friendly possesses an invisible ability to define and continue to uphold the status quo. Being a member of a preferred group that holds advantages makes it difficult for even the gay friendly and some Trump supporting queers, to countenance Trump’s attacks on LGBTQ. Straight, but gay friendly people, whose sexuality was never “caused” by psychological trauma, sin, or abuse, have never been targeted for hate and are insulated by recent queer-abolishing cuts to LGBTQ health care. While the subject of privilege must reflect on its many facets and contradictions—I am indeed writing about privilege as a gay but white, cis-gender, middle class, male—according to Kie Hart, not having to think of or even consider this peril is literally defining social norms and “distributing advantages based on hierarchy.” This, she concluded, allows “the [supposedly straight] holder of privilege to choose whether to object to oppression.”  

A binary of (hetero-) privilege and the unprivileged emerges. Queer people, with relatively less social capital to advance their own rights, rely on some straight people to advance them. The sexual minority in this case, can’t exist absent its antagonistic other, where heterosexuality is more valued and rightly belongs in the social world, Kie Hart writes. This privilege, she continues, masks its power over the unprivileged, and less valued, in comparison. Put differently, a good part of queers living openly and freely comes about when straight people consciously choose equal rights for them.

But an obstacle to straight people choosing freedom for queers, Kie Hart argues, is that they depend on queers to remain “divided, fearful, and suspicious of each other” to remain in power. The gay friendly situated on top of the gender orthodoxy are motivated to remain in the advantaged group. Shielded by Trump attacks on LGBTQ, they only have a shaky tendency to object to its injustice. With queers enforcing the rules of this orthodoxy themselves, for the gay friendly group subordination stabilizes their own prevalence, power, and authority. Straight presentation manifesting substantially more social legitimacy and control of the societal apparatus of force and as a socially-aligned community, can consensually associate power with a variety of high status social institutions, say Felicia Pratto et al. The nuclear family, religious doctrine, our education and workplace cultures, etc. all need queers, with relatively less institutional power, to uphold the illusion of compulsory heterosexuality. Inequality, Kie Hart argues dishearteningly, is here to stay. 

Or maybe not. Completely. Pratto et al. argues that dominance is maintained by institutional discrimination, cultural ideologies and force, but these practices do not guarantee dominance is maintained or that societies are unchangeable. Which brings me to the last consequence to queer life which I have already illustrated with the rather improbable, ally of queer. Queers depend to a large degree on both straight and gay people willingly ceding some of their own social power, to exist. Only a queer-straight coalition has the needed power to advance social justice and this alliance, as it would be, has historically pushed back on oppression globally. It constitutes a political backbone that has led to a general increase in LGBTQ freedom. 

Says Kie Hart, allyship is an action that de-centers, reveals, and resists privilege. An ally of queer is someone who wouldn’t let a homophobic comment within their own social circle, ride. They see, rather unexpectedly, queer oppression and expend some of their own social capital in its face. Kie Hart says an ally is someone who chooses “strength and empowerment rather than defeat and discouragement.” They willingly transfer some of the benefits of their own privilege, in a rather dubious moment of opportunity, to those who lack it “regardless if oppression is ever fully eradicated.” 

I wasn’t about to abandon my own personal interest to protect those of Riley. I might have seemed trans-friendly to Adam, her pre-transition name, because he trusted me enough to share his gender dysphoria. But honestly, I was probably only tolerant. Judging by my own awkward silence when Adam talked about it, I was uncomfortable with the idea that someone would go to medical lengths to change their birth-assigned gender, dysphoria or not. I suppose my attitudes were more or less in line with many in the gay community who view trans as overly radical.

But more, I felt Riley’s transition would always have an ersatz quality to it. Read female perhaps in some circumstances but importantly, never completely passable. She had to pass without detection, which I knew many trans people did, for her transition to be “successful.” Riley would “look trans” which to my gay discernment, was more like a drag performance. Sure, it was wickedly transgressive of femininity, but her detectable status would give it a temporary aura that was always regressing back to her “true” gender. 

But my relationship with her would challenge this partial definition of passability which was making her gender identity illegitimate––a form of erasure. Riley’s body was not incidental in its dissent from the “official” gender binary. Yes, it joyfully transgressed from gender rules not unlike drag, but crucially her femaleness was an intrinsic joyfulness that was self-generated from the inside. It was the personhood she naturally wanted to share with others as much as I quite unconsciously did as a man. Riley told me she felt gender dysphoria “the most when someone in the real, outside world misgenders me.” “When there is incongruity between how I think others should see me and how people actually do. When I get this wrong. It hurts.” 

To freely be the woman she is with others was a freedom owed to Riley. Getting misgendered was a violation of her dignity which curbed her personal autonomy. She told me that when “people use the new, correct pronouns for me,” when they “see me as a woman when I assume they would not… this is elating.” This elation came from the natural feeling of participating in public life. When some of my fellow cis friends make fun of correct gender pronouns, this could be my opportunity to be an ally. To show them as Dr. Davis describes it, my “whole-hearted embrace” of Riley. I could leverage my cisgender ranking to punch holes in the gender binary that is also simultaneously striving, she noted, for a culture that “cultivate[s] widespread understanding, respect, and justice.” Allies, she concluded, “take the lead” in doing this by calming nerves about someone for whom the majority finds odd or strange. I could turn the complexity of gender expression into a genuinely-funny trans joke maybe. If I did it, this would put my status to use as an inclusive action which was a primary task in a democracy.

by Ann John

On March 28, 2025 an appellate court judge cleared the legal path for President Trump to dismantle the U.S. Agency for International Development (USAID).  

Like a broken clock getting the time right, Trump is correct that USAID should not exist. But not for his reasons. Contrary to Trump’s assessment that USAID does nothing for Americans, the agency arguably does more for the U.S. than for recipient countries. The U.S. is both the arsonist and firefighter in the Global South and it’s time for USAID to grapple with the harms it’s done in the name of doing good. 

Amidst the daily scandals of the second Trump administration, the defunding of USAID has become synonymous with Trump’s executive overreach. USAID cuts are mentioned in the same breath as the other federal jobs headed for Musk’s shredder. Though factual, this framing suggests that fighting for USAID is an act of liberal resistance equal to saving the Postal Service. But USAID is unlike other agencies. My mail carrier has never normalized Israeli colonization of Palestine nor partnered with the Central Intelligence Agency to train foreign police in torture.  

USAID is state-sponsored reputation laundering. Kathryn Mathers, a professor at Duke University who has worked on USAID-funded literacy projects, says that the agency “in many ways produces [global inequality],” by “hiding the ways … U.S. policies, U.S. trade agreements and other forms of extractive capitalism are often the causes [of poverty].”  

Our current political chaos overlooks how USAID keeps the Global South poor. Decades of research shows that foreign aid keeps countries dependent by killing local production. The free aid floods the local market, and drives down the price of goods. As a result, local producers have to sell their goods at a loss and are eventually driven out of the market entirely. For instance, after the 1976 earthquake in Guatemala, the US’s “gift” of 27,000 metric tons of wheat depressed food prices. The Guatemalan government responded by barring further imports of grain.  

Despite the body of evidence, USAID continues food aid programs because it benefits American farmers. The USAID program Food for Peace is intended to sell or donate American agricultural surplus. “Someone always gets rich off a famine,” said Michael Moren, former food aid monitor for USAID Somalia. USAID makes sure it’s American farmers who profit from famine.  

USAID’s alignment with American political goals hinders its humanitarian aims. Congress requires the President’s Emergency Plan for AIDS Relief (PEPFAR), which is implemented by USAID, to spend one-third of the $120 billion it has received since 2003 on abstinence-only programming. The approach has never lowered rates of sexual disease. Worse, research shows that abstinence only programs make the fight against HIV harder by promoting medically inaccurate information. Who knew spreading misinformation was part of the “life saving” work USAID did.  

If PEPFAR has mixed results, why has it continued to receive bipartisan support? The program cleans founder former President George W. Bush‘s image.Since he was a Texas governor, Bush is guided by his philosophy of compassionate conservatism, an image rehabilitation program to associate Republicans with “compassion” rather than “heartlessness” and “tax-cut obsessed.” Just like USAID washes Americas’ reputation, PEPFAR rehabilitates Republican’s image.  

Democrats consistently oppose abstinence-only education in the U.S. Why are they allowing it to be taught in the Global South?  

This is not to say that PEPFAR is all bad. Twenty-five million people, like children infected at birth and refugees raped by soldiers, have been treated for HIV. But the good done for individuals does not erase the harm done systematically to recipient countries.  

Historically, critiques about the short-term nature of USAID programs have been brushed aside by pulling on heartstrings. The Agency responded to opposition with the stories of the 1 million Rohingya refugees densely packed together in the world’s largest refugee camp. The meanings? Esoteric critiques pale in the face of starving children.  

The State Department’s justification for the cuts is that USAID has no “return for the American people.” The accusation has caused supporters to abandon moralistic language and say the quiet part out loud. USAID helps Americans. American wheat, soybean, and peanut farmers wrote op-eds explaining how USAID provides jobs and a market for surplus product. Protest signs read “USAID: A National Security Investment,” alluding to supporters’ beliefs that China, Russia, and Iran will fill the spot on the international stage that America vacated. Development organizations tattled on themselves by admitting that “a lot of the [USAID] money starts out with American organizations staffed by Americans.”  

USAID is not a charity for the Global South. It is a way for liberals to soothe their guilt and play white savior.     

With USAID gone, there is the space for progressives to radically rethink development. Typical alternatives to USAID are other state or international actors, or the free market. But all of these “solutions” continue to privilege elites in the Global North and South, and the existing unfair economic order. James Ferguson, a scholar of development at Stanford, has two alternatives: advocating against American imperialists policies and connecting with counter-hegemonic organizations abroad. The former is a preventative solution, as the U.S. is often the source of development issues. This means changing U.S. intellectual property laws, because they increase global health inequalities like the vaccine apartheid. The latter entails connecting with labor or peasant unions, opposition parties, cooperatives, or religious organizations, to assist with existing goals and projects. The solution to global inequality has never been a Westerner starting a new 501(c)(3).  

The end of foreign aid can have positive effects. The head of Africa CDC, Dr. Jean Kaseya, considers the USAID funding freeze “a wake up call” and “an opportunity for us to rethink how African countries take the lead.” Dr. Kaseya is correct that stopping foreign aid can turn countries into leaders, rather than dependents. Research shows how rejecting foreign aid increases a country’s prestige. Wanting to graduate from being a helpless victim factored into India’s, Pakistan’s and Kenya’s decision to reject aid in the mid 2010s. A two decade retrospective on India’s decision to reject aid after a tsunami speaks to the country emerging as a regional leader in disaster response. India is now a regional leader in tsunami warning and a donor of international aid to Sri Lanka, Indonesia, and Thailand. 

“Aid could be worse than incompetent and inadvertently destructive. It could be positively evil,” said Maren after witnessing food aid prolonging the Somali civil war. When those on the ground say that aid is evil, it is past time to defend USAID.

by Patrick McGee

Image: Toyen, Untitled. 1939

What is a community? A place? A time? Is it constituted of tangible ephemera? Or is it rather imagined, found in memory? In “Sense of Community: A Definition and Theory,” an influential psychology piece by David W. McMillan and David M. Chavis, community is defined in four parts: membership, influence, integration and fulfillment of needs, and shared emotional connection. Through the cultivation of the feeling of belonging and reciprocity among members, communities may participate in vibrant cultural practice and preservation, and the collective formation of meaning. Community archives, then, are defined by archival theorists Anne Gilliland and Andrew Flinn as “diverse, real-world interventions into the field of local, regional and national even international archival and heritage narratives, often critical interventions, politically charged with notions of social justice and civil rights,” collapsing distinctions between any hegemonic understanding of archives towards one embedded in a people. One of these communities in search of an archive was the community of jazz musicians who made their home between Corona and St. Albans in Queens. This neighborhood, as we will see, was a bastion of creativity and a historic site for Black American art.

Jazz music is the sound of freedom. The music consists of a critique of dominant culture alongside a form of ironic transcendence, referred to as quotation. When you play a well-known melody in a new way, repurposed and reclaimed, it takes on new meanings – tradition is transformed into freedom. There is a deathly serious edge running along the mélange of American life – the liberation of people through American song and African rhythm is certainly one of our greatest traditions. Jazz musicians are a community of people courageously writing themselves, the music an invention of new references at once ancient and futurist, popular and obscure. We may call this a “common symbol system,” as McMillan and Chavis theorize an essential element of community cohesion. These mechanisms (manner of dress, speech, other cultural practices) serve to define a community’s boundaries, thus establishing its meaning as a single unit in time and space. For these reasons, we may understand jazz music and its creators as a long-standing Black American community, whose migration and development are woven through slavery, emancipation, and the temporal tidal wave of the 20th century.

As a part of CUNY Cultivating Archives and Institutional Memory, a 3-year Mellon Foundation funded initiative to develop a centralized archival mechanism at CUNY, I have been privileged to experience the breadth of CUNY’s archival holdings. It is no exaggeration to say that the sum of the collections is the history of New York. Most weeks, a team of twelve of us visit a different campus, opening every box in their archives to find hidden traces of CUNY history, providing them with a survey of their collection. This survey is part of the project’s mission to explore, unify and raise awareness and use of CUNY’s vast archival collections. I hope to write further on the nature of this project, but I will trace here a specific archival encounter, both to tease out the politics of preservation, as well as to highlight what I believe to be a very important collection.At York College, a coworker and I were to work on the Black American Heritage Foundation Music History Archive, an independent archive within York College documenting the lives of jazz musicians from the neighborhood of St. Albans. We wound our way through the labyrinth of York College in search of this potential gem. Up and down staircases, dead-end hallways, myriad elevators, a DJ playing songs from 2008, a basement lunch nook…Ultimately, we found a security guard with keys, and a door was unlocked. We passed through a large room walled-of windows and filled with unused office furniture. As we met people involved with the archive, we learned that multiple departments had made claims upon this space, but that nothing had ever come to pass. It was a room awaiting occupants; as we were to learn, it was also a place containing a community’s treasure.

. . .

The story of the Music History Archive is impossible to tell without the story of its founder, Clarence Irving, Sr. Irving’s self-historicizing is energetic; his life, the meaning of resilience (I recommend this oral history conducted through the Brooklyn History Center). His great-great-great-great-great grandfather was one of the first twenty Africans kidnapped and brought to America by the Dutch in 1619. His father, a former slave, worked in the Navy Yard during the Spanish-American War. His was a “Navy Yard family,” and Clarence joined this lineage in 1944, working in the shipyard until after the Korean War. He then worked for transit, in machine shops, and as an electrician until his retirement. Throughout his life, Irving organized his community. The first instance we know of Irving’s community work was the founding of a community baseball team in Jamaica, Queens. Called The Bisons, the team was formed in response to seeing police break up a neighborhood game. In 1964 the Bisons became a chartered athletic club and began to collaborate with other organizations to promote education initiatives and community building. Out of this initial organization, the Bisons Bicentennial Committee emerged in 1976. The Committee would be instrumental in the formation of the Black American Heritage Trail, a memory-work project mapping the early history of black life in New York City. Irving and the Bicentennial Committee were also integral to the creation of the United States Postal Service’s Black Heritage stamp series; Harriet Tubman became the first African American woman to appear on a US postage stamp in 1978. In 1984, the Bisons Athletic Club was renamed the Black American Heritage Foundation (BAHF) as its work expanded. The Black American Heritage Foundation’s founding mission was to:

document, preserve and disseminate information about the accomplishments of African Americans, assist young people to develop educationally, culturally, morally and socially; and inculcate in our young the spirit of good citizenship and full awareness of the cultural heritage of African Americans.

The Music History Archive was founded in 1989. Irving developed the project as a joint venture between the BAHF and York College. He presented the idea to Claire Paisner, at that time the director of public information at York College. Dr. Robert Parmet, a professor in the History and Philosophy department, was another early advocate and collaborator. Conceived as a community archive within the institution, Irving’s mission, as described in Parmet’s wonderful essay, “Clarence Irving and the Rediscovery of Black America,” was “to preserve the music legacy of African Americans especially those who had resided or were still residing in the area” of Jamaica, between Corona and St. Albans. This work began in the 1970s, Irving curating concerts devoted to the music of the community which at various times included Louis Armstrong, Count Basie, and other luminaries of Black American Music. Irving was also a devotee of the pianist and composer Duke Ellington and held annual concerts at York College to celebrate Ellington’s birthday.

. . .

Over the course of our work, we were warmly engaged by the current steward of the archive, Professor Mark Adams of the Music Department. Adams teaches music theory, piano techniques, keyboard harmony, jazz techniques and improvisation at York, and is a long-time member of the CUNY community, receiving his Bachelor of Fine Arts in Music Performance from City College, and a Master of Arts from Queens College. His passion for the archive was infectious; as we sorted and arranged sprawling cardboard boxes of papers donated by the archive’s founder and various jazz musicians, Adams brought three more faculty by to see – or rather, to feel – the potential of this collection. It was clear that when people are confronted with real archives – that function, that trace, that in-between of memory and amnesia where the past becomes present and floods the moment with meaning, they are overwhelmed with the spirit of futurity and seek to understand their own lives through the materials. In research for this article, I had the pleasure of speaking to Adams on the phone, whose joyful spirit carried across the digital distance. At one point, he played “All the Things You Are” for me on the piano, a real pleasure and privilege. As we sorted through the boxes, the importance of this collection for the Queens jazz community was palpable – there were old tuxedos and suitcases from trumpeter Buck Clayton’s stint in the Count Basie Orchestra, shellac vinyl wrapped in green velvet, original sheet music of the beloved bassist Milt Hinton, best known for his stints in the Cab Calloway Orchestra alongsidebebop innovator Dizzy Gillespie (and, importantly, Irving’s next-door neighbor). And while the musical scores, ephemera and instruments were unique and notable, in some ways it was the archive itself – the lost history of its founding, its tenacity and perseverance, its purpose as a community archive – that was most impactful. The neighborhood of St. Albans is renowned for its musical scene – from John Coltrane to A Tribe Called Quest, a seemingly endless line of luminaries found a home here, something Irving clearly hoped to promote and preserve.

In an article in the York College newsletter Pandora’s Box from the time of the archive’s founding, Claire Paisner is quoted: “The archive is a mecca. A thing of both local and national significance.” Parmet stated in this same article, “It’s a community awaiting discovery…it is one of the most interesting things the college has ever done.” The Black American Heritage Foundation Music History Archive remains a community awaiting discovery. In a conversation with Adams, there is work being done to partner the archive with York’s archival materials on its public art, a collaboration with Emily Verla Bovino, Assistant Professor and Coordinator of the Art History program at York. Bovino stressed the importance of the late Margaret Rose Vendryes, former Chair of the Department of Performing and Fine Arts and Director of the Fine Arts Gallery at York College, to the archive, and as the inspiration for the developing relationship between the Music History Archive and the Art History program’s work documenting public art on York College’s campus. Adams and Bovino have been awarded funding by York College to digitize the collection’s audio-visual materials – VHS tapes, U-Matics and cassettes – with CUNY TV , an exciting opportunity to preserve materials that would otherwise deteriorate and cannot be watched or listened to without digitization due to their fragility. Bovino stated that, “the archive not only helps us to understand Jamaica of that period, but it supports Jamaica residents in their desire to learn from lessons of the past in their efforts protecting the distinct character of the neighborhood under current real estate and urban planning pressures.” She cited the local Southeast Queens Center for History & Culture and Southeast Queens Artist Alliance and their interest in working with York’s archives in their programming. Alongside digitization, a process of archival accessioning, arrangement, and description must occur, and a proper facility must be found. It is my hope that in highlighting this collection, local historians and community members will advocate for the Music History Archive so that the work necessary to preserve it can be carried out.

Parmet wrote in his essay on Irving:

Nearly three decades after its founding, the York College-Black American Heritage Foundation Music History Archive is housed in the college library, awaiting its permanent home in a future Academic Village and Conference Center on the school’s campus. When relocated it will better serve students, scholars, tourists, and anyone else interested in discovering the amazing contributions of the African American musical artists of Southeast Queens.

As I basked in the sound of Adams’ masterful piano stylings, and considered the potentials for this community archive, I was taken by how much love there is in the York College arts community. I was moved by Adams’ impassioned statement in our conversation: “I want [the archive] to be seen by the world.” Because Adams and Bovino have so much love for their work, it will undoubtedly fulfill Irving’s dream of becoming a home for community history. When archival work is done with dedication and style, the archive comes to life — this was my experience in the Black American Heritage Foundation Music History Archive. The archive is a testament and a promise; there are future archive stories to be written.

Much of the historical information in this essay is drawn from Robert Parmet’s essay, Clarence Irving and the Rediscovery of Black America (2018). I am grateful to Mark Adams, Lecturer in Music at York College, and Dr. Emily Verla Bovino, Assistant Professor of Art History at York College, for their willingness to discuss and provide access to the collection.

By Bîrgul Das

“Heta azadiyê em nebînin, Li xwe nakin kincê bûk zavan e.”

Hozan Serhad was a freedom fighter and a musician. The last years of his life were spent in the mountains, both singing and fighting to defeat the colonizer. Just like a lot of Kurdish artists, he used more than strength to defend his people. His art was another way for him to express the need for freedom within the struggle. At the middle of his career, he decided that the mountains were his purpose in life, defending his country from aggressors and dedicating his life to the struggle. He played a major role in keeping Kurdish music alive, singing classic Kurdish songs and influencing other artists about its importance. He was aware of the government’s assimilation policies, and the Turkification of Kurdish culture deeply troubled him. His resistance was against both physical and cultural oppression.

Hewlêr has all the fundamental elements that define Kurdish music. Pain, sorrow, resistance, mourning and love for Kurdistan are all present in it, making Hewlêr a quintessential representation of Kurdish music. The opening track, Çarin features the tembûr—a traditional stringed instrument that Hozan Serhad knew how to play, along with the saz, guitar, keyboard, and pipe. Without any lyrics, Çarin makes itself one of the contenders for the best song of the album. The beautiful, hypnotic sound of the tembûr, with each plucked string, carries the weight of his unspoken stories––the best intro that could have been made for the album Hewlêr.

In the second track, Hozan Serhad talks about another revolutionary—an artist and a guerrilla like himself, Hozan Mizgîn. She was the first woman from her city to join the resistance and was both a founding member of Koma Berxwedan and a key figure in what would become one of the most influential musical groups in Kurdistan. In the song, Hozan Serhad repeats Mizgîne leheng, Mizgîne çeleng, meaning Hero Mizgîn, strong Mizgîn, as her bravery influenced millions of Kurdish people—especially Kurdish women. She became a martyr by taking her own life rather than surrendering to the enemy—an act honored by Hozan Serhad, who sings, Şêra me Kurdan silav da Tetwan, meaning, The lion of the Kurds saluted Tetwan.

 The third track, Ax Kurdîstan, stands as a dedicated testament to the depth of his feelings for his homeland. “Kurdistan, Your plains and branches are colourful, Like gardens of flowers, Oh My nation, Your workers are rebellious, Like heroes…” These lyrics reflect the voice of a freedom fighter who declared “For a revolutionary, returning to the country is a duty.” He held a deep love for his homeland—its mountains, its landscapes, and its people—and never hesitated to sing about them. 

He was also no stranger to the suffering—nor to the endurance––that freedom demands. His stories also spoke of sufferings, exiles, tortures, and betrayals. The self-titled track Hewlêr reflects one of the massacres that deeply affected him, and through it, he aimed to convey those sufferings and betrayals. “Hewlêr, mourning of the mothers, screams of the children, kohl of the brides, blood of the martyrs, You turned your glory into resistance…” The lyricism of Hewlêr reflects the profound impact of this betrayal, the pain deepened by the fact that it was his own people who sided with the enemy— an artist’s expression of collective grief.

Freedom fighters say, “An artist is not someone who simply reaps the benefits of what is created, but one who plays an active role, contributing their labor, sweat, and blood to every value created.” This holds particular significance for oppressed communities, where art has historically served as a potent form of resistance. This was profoundly true for the Kurdish people, whose art held such power that it became the target of systematic erasure. This is where artists like Hozan Serhad come into play, using their music and storytelling as a means of preserving culture, defying oppression, and ensuring that their people’s history and struggles are never forgotten. This very aspect positions Hewlêr as not just an album, but fundamentally an act of resilience.

Text and images by Meg Kaizu

“Wanderer above the Sea of Fog” (1818)

This article will explore Caspar David Friedrich’s artworks featured in “Caspar David Friedrich: The Soul of Nature” at the Metropolitan Museum, as an attempt to think about Romantic thought and aesthetic concepts such as the sublime and the picturesque. In what follows, I will discuss the geographical features of Friedrich’s landscapes to suggest that there are parallels between the aesthetic ideas and motifs in his works and those of Eastern artistic traditions, drawing on “Suuko no bigaku / 崇高の美学 (Aesthetics of the Sublime)” by Hideki Kuwajima.

Caspar David Friedrich (1774–1840) was a German painter who re-conceptualized European landscape painting by portraying nature as a setting for deep spiritual and emotional contemplations and insights. The Romantic movement championed an innovative understanding of the bond between nature and our inner self. As a Romantic artist, Friedrich developed pictorial subjects and strategies, underscoring the individuality, intimacy, open-endedness and complexity of human response to the natural world. The landscape meditatively and mysteriously unfolds in his art, often inspiring wonder and awe in viewers, revealing the shifting developments in how nature was viewed in the Western world, from the Romantic period to contemporary times. The oil paintings, drawings, and working sketches from various phases of Friedrich’s career in the exhibition illuminate how he developed a symbolic vocabulary of landscape motifs to represent the personal and spiritual meanings that he found in nature. The exhibition positions Friedrich’s art within the politics and culture of 19th-century German society, highlighting the role of Romanticism in shaping modern perceptions of the natural world.

“Morning Mist in the Mountains” (1807-8) represents a misty view of the mountaintop, painted in oil on canvas. The mountain appears to dissolve among tendrils of vapor gradually clearing around the summit. On top of the mountain, a tiny cross is visible against the blue sky, as if to suggest that divinity is discernible only to those who seek it. The landscape looks mystical and spiritual. Friedrich gravitated toward motifs of cloud and fog because he thought that they enhanced the mystery and grandeur of the landscape. The delicate layers of mist in this painting also reveal his enthusiasm for oil painting as a medium he had mastered around the time he made this painting.

“Ruins at Oybin” (ca. 1812) depicts an abandoned medieval monastery painted in oil on canvas. Friedrich made a sketch of this site before he painted this piece. In this painting he elongated the walls and added several elements to the earlier sketch, such as a statue of the Virgin Mary and Christ Child, a crucifix, an abandoned altar supported by angels and symbolic plants such as the lily (often used to represent the Virgin Mary’s purity). In the Romantic period, abandoned religious buildings were symbols of both the fragility and the continuity of faith. Many Catholic buildings in Germany had been abandoned after the Protestant Reformation in the 16th century. Visual references to the Middle Ages and cultural artifacts such as the ruins in his paintings could be viewed as something that links the distant past to the present—almost like an emblem of what could be lost and found again to give a new meaning continuously. “Ruins at Oybin” captures both picturesque and gothic aesthetics, representing medieval ruins and serving as a reminder of past human presence. It is a moody, nostalgic and romantic scenery that has traces of human life and nature mixed and juxtaposed together.  

“Wanderer above the Sea of Fog” (1818) depicts a man on a rocky precipice overlooking the foggy scenery beneath him. The mystical landscape invites various interpretations, giving this painting a sense of ambiguity. Evoking a sense of beauty and danger, mystery and uncertainty, the artwork has become an iconic visual representation of the Romantic movement. It is considered one of the Romantic masterpieces and thought to visually represent the aesthetic concept of the sublime. Friedrich was a common user of a compositional device Rückenfigur (Rear-facing figure) in his artworks. It is somewhat ambiguous as to whether the artist invites identification or encourages second-order observation in “Wanderer above the Sea of Fog.” The interpretation is left open-ended, much like the aesthetics of the sublime broadly and specifically in this artwork. Here Friedrich allows for viewers to interpret his use of Rückenfigur in an open-ended manner. Similarly, the aesthetic concept of the sublime is ambivalent and “Wanderer above the Sea of Fog” holds space for viewers to explore their own thoughts and feelings to wonder about the experience of the sublime.

“Dolmen in Autumn” (ca. 1820) depicts an ancient megalithic structure against a bleak autumn landscape with an approaching storm. It is painted in oil on canvas. Friedrich first sketched a dolmen in 1802 near his birthplace in Greifswald. Viewed in its historical context––the wake of French invasion of Germany in the early 1800s, and the repressive monarchies established afterward––the landscape may represent Friedrich’s thoughts and feelings for his country. Viewed this way, the dolmen in an autumn storm may convey an enduring past of his homeland and its history and continuity into modern times. Friedrich submitted this painting as a reception picture to mark his membership for the Dresden academy.

“New Moon or Solar Eclipse above the Riesengebirge” (ca. 1828) was painted in ink and watercolor over pencil on wove paper. In this piece, Friedrich painted a view of the Giant Mountains in a particular light. The luminous planet in the sky, which had long been identified as a new moon (one of Friedrich’s favorite motifs), has recently been recognized as a solar eclipse. It is the moon obscuring the sun. The annular solar eclipse is known to have taken place in 1820. The symbolism of the solar eclipse as a peculiar, uncanny astronomical phenomenon conveys the complex history of this region; since the Middle Ages, a state border has been established in the Giant Mountains, first between Poland and Bohemia, then between the Polish Duchy of Jawor and Bohemia, between Prussia and Austria, between Germany and Czechoslovakia, between Poland and Czechoslovakia, then between Poland and the Czech Republic. The unsettling view of the solar eclipse may serve to remind viewers of these historical and political changes and the uncertain fate of the land through centuries.

“The Riesengebirge” (ca. 1830-1835) is painted in oil on canvas. It captures the Giant Mountains in undulating shades of green, brown and gray that recede into the distant space and the horizon. The muted earth tones provide a foil for the nuanced tints of the sky. The landscape looks uninhabited at first, but a closer look shows a man seated on a rock to the right of the trees. The man appears as a tiny figure, as if lost in the layered, boundless landscape. Friedrich’s skill to depict the mountain range in nuanced shades is masterful. His composition capturing a spectacular view of the mountains, while holding a human presence in the foreground, suggests Friedrich’s thoughts on humanity’s relationship and unity with nature. Considering the complex history of the region and changing borders, viewers may feel as though human understanding and history is narrow and limited, especially when compared to nature’s timeless, boundless and ahistorical presence.

“A Walk at Dusk” (ca. 1830-1835) features dolmen and new moon, two of Friedrich’s favorite motifs, accompanied by Venus. It is painted in oil on canvas. The cloaked figure, potentially Friedrich himself, appears to be praying as if to mourn the bygone time. The ancient grave marker appears to symbolize the enduring artifact and material culture that survives through millennia. Dolmen may serve as a visual reference and connection that brings his people and the ancient past together. Friedrich might have viewed the prehistoric past as an era when the ancients lived more in harmony with nature, compared to how people did in Europe in the 19th century. The cloaked figure appears deeply contemplative by the dolmen, possibly reflecting on temporality, human history, human life and natural history.

“Dolmen near Gützkow” (ca. 1837) is painted on wove paper in brown ink and wash with pencil. Friedrich first sketched a dolmen in 1802 and painted it in several other works. In this piece, he presented it as a solitary rock on a hilltop against an open sky, focusing on the visual representation of the rock formation. It depicts the irregular surfaces, negative spaces, and striking combination of mass and equilibrium, and the large stone strangely balanced on much smaller stones. The subdued, monochromatic treatment of the landscape prompts viewers to notice the textures and details of the landscape. The landscape without any visible traces of human presence may indicate a natural history which continues by itself, at its own pace, without human intervention, almost lacking a sense of time.

“Dolmen near Gützkow” (ca. 1837)

Sublime places of the East could be found in the moist, lush mountains covered in mist. Confucius mentions that people who possess ren (仁 / humanness) love mountains and wise people love water. In East Asia, historically, landscapes with clouds, mountains and rocks represented the spiritual world. Kuwajima suggests that the image of xians living high up in the mountains represents the ideals of the sublime of East Asia. It could be argued that the Eastern sublime differs from the Western sublime, as far as it lacks a kind of ambivalence inherent in the Western aesthetic concept of the sublime. In the East, people don’t seem to hold ambivalent feelings toward the sublime mountains. As the Romantics wanted to integrate intellect and sensibility, it might have been the expression of the sublime visually and conceptually closer to their visions.

In “Suuko no bigaku,” Hideki Kuwajima introduces the story of Boyi and Shuqi known to have been embraced by Confucius. The older brother Boyi refused to take over the rule of his father’s kingdom because he felt his father preferred his younger brother Shuqi. Shuqi refused the rule because it would be unfilial to allow his older brother to be bypassed. This led the two brothers to flee together. After the overthrow of the Shang dynasty, to which they had pledged loyalty, the two brothers faced the dilemma of disloyalty in eating the food of the new dynasty or remaining loyal in spirit to the former dynasty. The two were left with starvation as the final option in the mountains. Boyi and Shuqi have had a long legacy in philosophy and literature, as well as art and poetry in East Asia.

Orientalism was a Western scholarly discipline in the 18th  and 19th centuries, and Chinoiserie influenced various aspects of European cultures such as gardens and architectural and decorative arts. The Great Pagoda at Kew Gardens in England, Oranienbaum Palace in Germany, and Meissen porcelain are some of the examples. Chinoiserie could be understood as a yearning for a better world, against the backdrop of Europe after the Seven Years’ War (1756–1763) and other wars of succession. It is against this backdrop that a yearning for peace and stability, a longing for a better life, could be understood. State leaders, philosophers and scholars needed to seek political solutions which would lead to peace and stability in Europe. The positive image of China shaped by the reports of the Jesuits might have been influential in how Europeans thought of Eastern traditions at that time.

“Ruins at Oybin” (ca. 1812)

There might have been a connection between the Romantic and non-Western aesthetic and ethical ideals. It is possible that the Romantics might have felt complex feelings towards the ways in which their world was changing. The story of Boyi and Shuqi is also a story about humans having to make choices that are political, moral and deeply personal in the face of dramatic historical changes. It is not difficult to imagine that European artists, particularly the Romantics, drew inspiration from various cultural artifacts, artworks, material cultures, and aesthetic and philosophical traditions of the Orient, seeking a “new community,” and trying to reimagine ways in which people could organize society in the aftermath of the French Revolution. They might have been looking for a different framework to integrate others, including nature and non-human animals.

There is something poignant about looking at and trying to engage with rocks and stones, which stay mute as geological processes and creations. In Japan, suiseki would be one of the ways in which people have culturally and aesthetically appreciated stones. Kuwajima writes that Da Vinci, Goethe, Kant, and Ruskin were “stone enthusiasts.” Friedrich might have been drawn to rocks and dolmen for the same reasons his “stone enthusiast” predecessors were. It would make sense then to look at Friedrich’s dolmen drawings and paintings as the artistic representations of his thoughts on megalithic ruins––the artifacts that endure through millennia. Friedrich was a liberal thinker who hoped for a democratic state for German-speaking people. Dolmen might have represented for him the megalithic structure that symbolizes the endurance, continuity and connections of his people from the ancient past to modern times.

“New Moon or Solar Eclipse above the Riesengebirge” (ca. 1828)

Mist and mountains are prominent motifs in Friedrich’s paintings. The Romantic era ushered in a new appreciation for mountains as sites of beauty and grandeur. Friedrich was also an avid hiker and channeled his perceptions, thoughts and feelings into his artworks. His midcareer paintings feature rocks, capturing its textures and structures from multiple vantage points. The ways in which the Eastern philosophers and artists thought of the misty mountains as an invigorating, life-giving space might have impacted Romantic thought on nature, among other influences. The sublime of the Eastern world differs from how the sublime was conceptualized in the Western world, but if the Romantics were looking for alternative expressions of the sublime and different ways to relate to nature, it might have been somewhat closer to the sublime that they could have been looking for.

This article examined Friedrich’s artworks to compare and contrast the Romantic representations and expressions of the sublime with Eastern artistic and philosophical traditions. I explored the geographical features of Friedrich’s landscapes to consider ways in which a few parallels could be drawn between the aesthetic concepts of the sublime in the West, and that of the Eastern philosophical traditions. Ultimately, I end this article by suggesting that the sublime experiences may continue to diverge cross-culturally in these two traditions and beyond, due to the long-standing unique and diverse philosophical developments and ways in which various traditions continue to view and relate to nature. Nevertheless, it is meaningful to observe and reflect on what the Romantics thought, felt and represented in their works at turbulent historical moments, to understand cultural and sociopolitical developments and how cross-cultural influences and conversations may happen when we attempt to draw inspiration from others.
