By Jennifer Welborn Williams

A premier wedding venue and luxury hotel stood in White Castle, Louisiana. The website overview says the resort was “one of the South’s largest historic mansions.” It was, in fact, a former sugar plantation called Nottoway Plantation, but the website does not mention much about that.  Nor does the website mention the enslaved people who lived and died there. The Nottoway Plantation burned to the ground on May 15, 2025, taking with it centuries of complicated history and anguish.

Built between 1857 and 1859 by enslaved Black craftsmen and artisans for an extremely wealthy Virginian named John Hampden Randolph, it became one of the largest sugar plantations in the Deep South. In 1860, John Randolph held 155 black people captive as slaves there.

The Emancipation Proclamation of 1863 technically freed slaves across the United States, but even after the end of the Civil War in 1865 most enslaved individuals were not really free. They continued to live and labor on the plantations where they had been enslaved, often for nothing more than a roof over their heads and food in their bellies.

Sharecropping became a way for wealthy planters to continue profiting off of black bodies while maintaining a façade of freedom. Former slaves would rent a parcel of land from the landowner and pay with a share of their crops.

That appears to be the case for many of the enslaved people who had nowhere else to call home but Nottoway Plantation.

The 1870 census sheds light on their story, and it is a story that deserves to be told. 

Living in numbered houses, houses which were likely the same houses that had been slave quarters prior to the Civil War, the census lists former slaves by family.

First, we have the Boon family. Hy Boon was 45 years old. His wife’s name was M. Ann, age 40. They were both born in Mississippi. They were purchased and brought from somewhere else to Louisiana. We don’t know where they were before they came to be at Nottoway. Hy is listed as a domestic servant and his wife was a housekeeper in the big house. Now she’s listed as keeping house, so she may simply be a housewife. Their daughter, Patsy, was 15. She was born in Louisiana. That means she was probably born on Nottoway Plantation, into slavery. Patsy is listed as a laborer. She also probably got to work mostly in the house because her parents were house slaves. House work does not mean an easier life. Closer proximity to the white family often meant more anxiety, and more opportunities for punishment.

Next, living together in Dwelling 525, we have the Fischer family. Keep in mind these “homes” likely consisted of a single room. The head of household was a man named Nick Fischer. He was 50 years old, and he was born in Virginia. John Hampden Randolph, the white planter who owned Nottoway, also came from Virginia. Therefore, it’s probable that Nick was brought to Louisiana with John Randolph. Nick is listed as a laborer, but we don’t know what kind of work he did. Catherine, age 45, is probably his wife. She has a hard job. She was a farm laborer. That’s back breaking work. She was also born in Virginia, and was probably brought to Nottoway with John Randolph. The rest of the Fischers were born in Louisiana. They are: Nick Jr., age 18, domestic cook; Andy (female), 23, keeps house; Angeline, 20, at home; Doney (female), 15, at home; and Louis, 17, laborer. 

 In Dwelling 526 we have two families residing together: the Smiths and the Taylors. It was not unusual to have multiple families crammed together under one roof. Francois Smith was a farm laborer. His wife, Adelaid, kept house. There was a toddler living with them. His name was James Fischer. He was 3 years old. Adelaid is probably his mother, but she could be an aunt. We don’t know. We don’t know what happened to his father. What we do know is this family has been separated and now there’s a new man in his life, Francois. This is not unusual, but it is sad.

The second family living here is another couple. The man’s name is George Taylor, and at the time of this census he was 37 years old. He is a farm laborer. His wife’s name is Jemy and she’s 30. She is also a farm laborer.

We can imagine fairly well what their lives looked like. Francois, George, and Jemy would have labored all day in the field just outside their one room home. Adelaid would have taken care of little James, cooked all the meals, washed clothing, and completed other house chores. It was not an easy life. But there was pride in no longer having to answer to an overseer and in knowing that the food you grew could be your own, even when there was absolutely still exploitation involved. 

In Dwelling 528 lives an old woman who had endured hardships we can only imagine. The name given on the census is Mathilde Domery and in 1870 she was 75 years old. Her birthplace is Africa. She was born around 1795. She traveled to America aboard a slave ship.

The name given to her at birth is lost to history, but there’s no way it was actually Mathilde.  Mathilde is a name foisted upon her by the people who colonized her body for profit. She had another name, an African name. One can hope she whispered it in secret to her children.

This elder survived the harrowing Middle Passage of the transatlantic slave trade. She survived the horrors of slavery and the Civil War. In 1870 she earned her rest, but instead of resting, she was tightly crammed into a one room home with other older former slaves to earn a plot of land instead. She is listed as a farm laborer. So are the others who reside with her: Diez Prouen, age 60, born in Mississippi; Harche Prior (male), age 55, born in Georgia; and Rebecca Evans, age 60, born in Virginia.

Every Dwelling tells a story, and there are many on the lands that held Nottoway Plantation, and throughout Louisiana. We should strive to tell them all.

By Meg Kaizu

 

Marvin Oliver (Quinault/Isleta Pueblo, b. 1946), Our River’s Ancestors, 2014.

Image via the National Museum of the American Indian––New York

 

An exhibition titled “Ancestral Connections” curated by Ann McMullen is currently on view at the National Museum of the American Indian––New York, the George Gustav Heye Center, featuring ten indigenous artists: Jackie Larson Bread, Gedion Fernandez, Anita Fields, Michael Massie, Marvin Oliver, Lillian Pitt, Jeri Redcorn, Isabel Rorick and Robin Rorick, Jim Schoppert, and Rose B. Simpson. The exhibition explores how the artists draw on various aspects of their heritage, sometimes combined with personal experiences or tribal history, as they create new and impactful works of art. The show demonstrates how a diverse group of indigenous artists respond to their traditional homelands and landscapes, traditional worldviews, lifeways and remembered ancestors, working with various artistic traditions and mediums. It reveals how the artists’ connections to their own cultures, traditions, heritage and histories are integral to contemporary Native artistic expression.

During my undergraduate studies, I took a course in American Indian Languages. I remember the professor said that the indigenous languages he taught didn’t have a word for “art.” He explained that this was because they didn’t distinguish “art” as something separate from other activities such as religion. Since I sat in his class that semester, I have thought about what he said, wanting to understand what “art” was. Each artist in “Ancestral Connections” engages with the themes of history, tradition, memory and heritage in varying ways, as they make art.

Marvin Oliver’s (b. 1946) “Our River’s Ancestors” (2014) is visually and conceptually compelling and poignant. In the piece, Oliver uses glass and paint to evoke the rivers and salmon that have intertwined with Quinault lives for millennia. The fish made of glass are luminous and glossy, and the bright red and light green add character to each salmon. Suspended in time and space inside a glass basket, each salmon appears to have a distinct personality, as though they are swimming in the timeless current that connects ancestors and descendants. A black-and-white photograph of fishermen is visible behind the salmon, indicating the cultural and intergenerational connections. Regarding his sculpture, Oliver says, “We feel that we are born from the rivers, that we are river salmon people.” The salmon represents both Quinault ancestors, and sustenance for Quinault people. The site where the picture was taken in the 1930s was submerged in 1957 by construction of the Dalles hydroelectric dam. Oliver also wants to encourage artists to study their own cultures, and I thought about how my engagement with Japanese artistic and cultural traditions have been an important part of my own writing and artmaking.

Anita Fields’s (b. 1951) “Sculpture” (1995) is made with pottery, glaze and plastic threads, as part of her “Native American Dresses” series. The piece represents a lovely dress in pastel pink, honoring indigenous women’s strength and resourcefulness, emphasizing the persistence of Native pride, dignity, and values in an ever-changing contemporary world. Fields is best known for her ceramics and textiles, and in “Sculpture” she brings the two mediums together. With her upbringing continually informing her creative process, Fields uses Osage worldviews as a metaphor, creating many of her art pieces based on the premise of Osage beliefs: the division of the earth and sky representing “the order, balance, and duality found in life, nature, and the universe.” The glazed pottery piece in the shape of a dress sewn together with plastic threads is a surprising and unique combination. It is thought-provoking that a pottery piece could be made to look like a dress, as though the material and medium could mimic textile art. “Sculpture” is aesthetically and conceptually intriguing for its medium, texture and hue. The lustrous buttons on the dress add elegance to the piece. I interpreted “Sculpture” as partly Fields’s commentary on the histories of pottery, textile and fashion, as well as Osage history.

Jackie Larson Bread’s (b. 1960) “Mirror Bag with Portrait of White Quiver” (1995) features a beautifully rendered portrait of the Blackfeet horse rider White Quiver in Hilde, glass beads, glass bells and satin. Bread describes her paintings as “highly rendered portraits” and her printmaking consists of “detailed etchings,” saying “creating photorealistic portraits from beads was a natural progression.” She uses traditional techniques but employs them in “a contemporary and evolving way.” Looking at her art pieces, I reflected on the boundaries of contemporary art and traditional techniques and craftsmanship. The mixing of the two (tradition and modernity) could be interpreted to mean Bread is drawing on her heritage in her own unique style, while her work is reflective of and responsive to the world we live in today. Beading is an interesting medium choice that I find compelling and suitable in “Mirror Bag with Portrait of White Quiver” because of its craft elements and labor. There is something meaningful about spending one’s time working and laboring to complete an art piece. The technique is not the kind of immediate process that gives us instant gratification but rather a slow, meditative one, in which we sit with the materials and reflect. I feel that it is what I enjoy in my own painting, bookbinding and collaging as well. I could photograph my subject matter in the moment but painting and collaging could capture and record time, thoughts and feelings at a much slower pace. As with Anita Field’s “Sculpture,” I think Bread’s “Mirror Bag with Portrait of White Quiver” plays with medium. It is a photorealistic portrait of White Quiver rendered in glass bead.

Rose B. Simpson’s (b. 1983) “Pod III” (2011) and “Pod IV” (2011) are made of pottery, reed, cotton twine and pigments. I was drawn to her pieces because of the sensitivity of the design of her baskets and how the baskets and human figures are contrasted with one another. I find the use of the mediums and the naturalistic color choices striking and delicate. Simpson, a Santa Clara Pueblo artist, says that “art is truly a part of everyday life. Your bowl, your chair, the way you walk – it’s not what you do but how you do it.” I thought of what my professor said in the American Indian Languages course. Art is not separate from everything else one does. Would that type of work be considered more of a craft, or is art more of our everyday life? I ruminated over the simplicity and rawness of Simpson’s baskets and ceramic figures perhaps because they feel close to my idea of the mundane, without heavy manipulation or alteration. Simpson made the pieces in a single studio session in the spirit of remaining true to the moment, keeping them somewhat imperfect, a fragile patchwork of components and influences. 

As a Warm Springs/Wasco/Yakama artist, Lillin Pitt (b. 1943) honors her ancestors, trying to give voice to her people, land and the animals of the land through her artmaking. In the 1980s, Pitt began using Japanese firing techniques and I thought it is an intriguing choice to bring another artistic and craft tradition to the indigenous artmaking. The result is Pitt’s unique, singular style. “Spirit of the Driftwood, No.10” (1982) is made of pottery feathers, commercial leather thong and glaze. “Mask” (1995) is made of pottery, glass beads, abalone shell beads, copper beads, metal wire and glaze. Both of her pieces are luminous and appear magical. Masks are associated with supernatural power across many different cultures, and that has been the case in traditional Japanese theater as well. I thought of Pitt’s mask representing the spirit of Driftwood, and how her art pieces appear to have magical power.

Michel Massie (b. 1962) brings his Inuit and Scottish heritage together in his work, expanding the bounds of what was perceived as Inuit art. Massie says he wishes viewers would focus on the art in “Inuit art,” adding “Art can be anything and that is true of Inuit art as well.” Massie’s “A Blind Man’s Vision” (2003) is made of limestone, tagua palm nut, caribou bone and ebony, depicting a blind hunter who offers a song to the owl spirit (shown on the reverse side), as he asks to have his sight restored for one last hunt. His piece made me think of Akira Kurosawa’s “Dersu Uzala” (1975), for it tells a story of a Nanai hunter whose failing sight hampers his ability to live as a hunter in taiga. Massie’s “The Look of Confidence Was Apparent (As He was About to Strike)” (2004) is made of limestone, cocobolo wood, ivory, caribou bone and sinew. Massie’s pieces ask uneasy questions about nature’s power and its destructive forces and the complex dynamics humanity has with nature, just as Kurosawa’s film asks similar questions.

After college, I went to Alaska for a theater internship, where I learned about the arts and storytelling of Tlingit. Since that time, I have reflected on how my grandparents’ traditional home, garden, ink-painting and calligraphy and my grandmother’s handmade kimono for our dolls, her origami and culinary skills, inspired my imagination. I also thought about how my travels and interactions with other cultures influenced my writing and artmaking. As an art teacher, I considered how I wanted to pass on my knowledge to the younger generations. As a writer and artist, I am interested in thinking about craftsmanship, materiality, skills, intergenerational knowledge and heritage. In “Archiving Cultures: Heritage, Community and the Making of Records and Memory,” Jeanette A. Bastian writes that heritage encompasses various human and societal expressions and activities – material, non-material and natural. She argues that heritage includes oral history, social practices, rituals, knowledge and skills passed on from generation to generation intra-communally, which differs from the established understanding of what heritage had been in the West. According to Bastian’s work, places and the environment are considered part of cultural heritage bringing together communal identity and the natural environment.

There is much diversity in the artworks featured in “Ancestral Connections,” in terms of the artists’ tribal affiliations, the mediums and materials, and what inspires and motivates them to make art. Citing the work of Maurice Halbwachs, Jeanette A. Bastian writes that memory is positioned as “both a socially constructed and a collective phenomenon” and every group has its own collective memory, which differs from the collective memories of other groups. While I think my personal engagement with Japanese culture has been integral to my artmaking, I also acknowledge that the ways in which each artist draws inspiration is personal and complex. Where we travel, who we meet, where we study, our environments and life events all influence the types and forms of art and subjects we are interested in exploring as artists, to varying degrees. 

During my undergraduate years, I thought about what beauty and aesthetics could mean for humanity, thinking about the differences between art and craft, wishing to know whether beauty and aesthetics were luxury or necessity. Reading “Defiant Gardens: Making Gardens in Wartime” by Kenneth I. Helphand, I came to think that people needed beauty. Helphand discusses how Japanese Americans created Japanese gardens in the internment camps during WWII, as an example of people wanting and needing beauty, even when they are faced with extreme, inhumane conditions in wartime.

Looking at the art pieces and learning about the artists in “Ancestral Connections,” I found myself deeply reflecting on each artist’s thoughts, feelings and visions and how diverse and personal their inspirations, visions and creative processes are. Some of the thought-provoking themes the artists raise are: the boundaries between art and craft, issues surrounding indigenous artmaking in the contemporary setting, how to engage with traditional artforms, what it means to make art to honor ancestors, how to reflect on heritage and tradition and think about art in the context of indigenous art and beyond, and the fact that indigenous art can be anything. I keep coming back to the questions of what art is and what art can be. I hope readers will visit the exhibition and engage with the artworks to think about some of these questions. The exhibit shows how the artists from various indigenous groups respond to personal and collective memory, wrestling with the questions of tradition and modernity in various artistic traditions, including non-indigenous art. The artworks in the show prompt viewers to think about how the artists’ connections to their cultures, heritage and histories serve as a catalyst for contemporary indigenous artistic expression.

Discontinued Studies,
The message is received.

Field of Study severed,
A voiceless, nameless villain speaks.

They decree,
“You are now a solo act.”

Who are they behind those titles? 
Like a chirping bird you sing. 

I dig in my heels,
Like a bull, I see the matador approach. 

My knowledge yearns for the Commons,
A pasture filled with my own
A tightening grip,
You transform into a bird of prey. 

Not this way,
They whisper again.

Your citations stray,
Their talons extend in anticipation. 

I stand firm,
They strike and I wince. 

Those sources are excess say they
strike again, a near miss. 

You lack voice,
Wildly scraping away at my thickening skin. 

Again I hold back, not knowing I could speak,
I dare not move. 

They hold out their conservative cloak,
Drenched in the blood of academic violence. 

A truth disguised,
Behind your acronyms and neologisms, there is the lie. 

But an ally charts a different course,
Out of the darkness, into the light. 

She shares her light
in the shadow of a rising sun.

Saying “forge your own trail” she shields, 
The predator retreats.

We stand together,
the bull learns to move on. 

The flame of inquiry burns
a new path lit by the stars, the sun sets. 

The night sky lit with colors,
We are no longer individualized, we continue as one.

From the Nursing Home Scandal to Sexual Harassment: Andrew Cuomo is Not the Savior we Need at Gracie Mansion

by Aida Lynn Eloumri

Attention all New Yorkers! Disgraced former Governor Andrew Cuomo has now entered back into the political arena. This time he is chasing a new role, becoming the next mayor of the Big Apple. Since he officially announced his candidacy on March 2nd,  Cuomo is now leading the polls with over 31% of supporters backing him as the Democratic nominee. New Yorkers are starting to question who they should vote for on June 24th, with the primary being crowded with candidates. Nonetheless, from lying to the general public about the deaths of nursing home residents during the pandemic, to the allegations made by thirteen women that he’d sexually harassed them, Andrew Cuomo is not the savior we need as mayor. 

Firstly, in the chaos of COVID-19 in 2020, Cuomo was perceived to be the calm during the storm with his daily press briefings, providing New Yorkers with up-to-date information on COVID-19 infection rates across counties, to the number of deaths the state saw each day. That trust has since been ruptured after news broke about nursing homes’ admitting patients regardless of COVID-19 diagnosis, as mentioned in the administrations’ March 2020 directive. Cuomo deliberately put the public health of those who were living in nursing homes at risk of contracting COVID-19. Reminder, this was the same guy who announced during his daily press conference that New Yorkers needed to social distance, wear masks when going out in public, and to get tested if you presented any symptoms. This is the perfect example of Cuomo being a walking contradiction. Not to mention, the administration reported that 8,505 long term care residents died from COVID as of January 2021, which is over 4,000 less than what was actually reported. I’m no mathematician, but intentionally undercounting the amount of people who died during a pandemic due to “…New York being one of the only states to count just those who died on facility grounds,…” is absolutely ludicrous and treacherous for public health. 

Secondly, within the same year that the lockdown was slowly being lifted in New York, another scandal came to light. Back in March 2021, former Cuomo employee Alyssa McGrath reported that she had been sexually harassed by the former governor, describing “..that Mr. Cuomo would ogle her body, remark on her looks, and make suggestive comments to her…”.  We are now living in a Me-Too/Time’s-Up society; people in power need to take accountability for their actions in the workplace. But McGrath was not the only one. Former aide to Governor Cuomo Charlotte Bennett spoke to the New York Times on how she was “…asked numerous questions about her personal life — comments she interpreted as clear overtures to a sexual relationship.” If you were at your job, and someone who has seniority over you had the audacity to ask you questions about your personal life in such an intrusive manner, you would think that’s inappropriate, too. So, why should we expect less from the candidate running for mayor? In 2024, Cuomo launched a defamation lawsuit against Bennett, claiming that she lied about being sexually harassed. Yes, because nothing screams “I’m innocent” more than a defamation lawsuit against your old colleague. Ultimately, this scandal was the final straw for Cuomo, as he resigned from being Governor of New York in August 2021. 

On the other hand, during his tenure as governor, he implemented decent policies that benefited a lot of New Yorkers. From passing the Climate Leadership and Community Protection Act, which aims for the state to be carbon neutral by 2050, to the implementation of comprehensive gun control through the New York Safe Act in 2013. Personally, I benefited from the Excelsior Scholarship initiative under Cuomo, which saved my family and I roughly $20,000 in college tuition. 

However, even the positive initiatives that he has implemented during his tenure as governor do not cover for the fact that Cuomo has been dishonest with the public during a worldwide pandemic and carried himself as a bully towards his staff and adversaries. Would you want a lying backstabbing bully to run the biggest economic and political hub in the country? I didn’t think so. 

With the Democratic primary election for New York City mayor only two and half months away, New Yorkers have a huge choice to make about our city’s future. But as Andrew Cuomo has proven to all New Yorkers time and time again, he is not the savior we need to lead our city come January 2026.

By Meg Kaizu

The exhibition ‘Nordic Utopia’  was organized by the National Nordic Museum in Seattle and ran at Scandinavia House, NYC from Nov 2024 to March 2025

 


The exhibition “Nordic Utopia? African Americans in the 20th Century” explores the under-told stories of black American artists who searched for new possibilities and inspiration in the Nordic countries. During the 20th century, black artists from the US visited, performed, studied, and lived in Scandinavia for various reasons such as a sense of adventure, love, educational and professional opportunities and freedom from segregation in the US. The exhibition at Scandinavia House looks at Denmark, Finland, Norway and Sweden as destinations for black American artists such as Ronald Burns, Doug Crutchfield, Dexter Gordon, William Henry Johnson, Howard Smith and Walter Williams. The exhibition includes a variety of artistic mediums such as paintings, music, sculpture and ceramics, as well as documentary evidence – photography, film and journalistic writing – to situate the artworks in art history of the 20th century. In this article, I will focus on three visual artists from the exhibition: Howard Smith, Ronald Burns and Walter Williams.

Howard Smith (1928–2021) was an artist and designer from New Jersey, who moved to Finland in 1962 and collaborated with Finnish design firms such as Vallila and Marimekko. I was intrigued by Smith’s artwork “Blue Irises” (1978) on stretched screen-printed cotton linen. It depicts seven blue irises with pale yellow spots, their dark stems and olive-green leaves arranged in a reddish-brown vase. I think the bold cool colors of the irises are impactful. As I looked at the details of the 50 x 27 canvas, I got a sense of Smith’s energy, curiosity and creative process. His watercolor painting “Untitled” (1971) represents an orange-red flower with its cool blue-green stem and leaves painted on handmade paper (28 7/8 x 22 1/8). Burns’s application of hues, temperature and intensity is distinct. Emily Stoddard, Manager of Exhibitions and Community Programs, who gave a gallery tour, mentioned that when asked why Smith painted flowers, he said that he felt he could paint anything. There was creative freedom that wasn’t available in the US. After arriving in Finland in 1962, Smith co-organized an international youth exhibition of American artists. A year after he arrived in Finland, Smith had the first show of his own at Matti Viherjuuri’s Galleria Pinx. He was attracted to the Finnish design aesthetic and tradition of craft and the handwrought object and won the respect of Finnish artists, architects and designers such as Kaj Frank, Aarno Ruusuvuori, Juhani Pallasmaa, Yrjö Sotamaa, and the Nurmesniemi’s, Antti and Vuokko. Smith was awarded the State Design Prize in Finland in 2001 and was recognized as Finland’s national treasure, receiving a state artist’s pension from 2003.

Roland Burns’s paintings “The Sky is Falling / Triumph of Nature I” (2006) and “The Sky is Falling / Triumph of Nature II” (2006) are exhibited side-by-side in the show. The two large-scale paintings (67 x 51  3/16) represent human figures in a surrealistic landscape, in a fragmented manner, with the rich details of plants, animals and man-made objects. I think the mediums Burns chose––pencil, watercolor and gouache––allowed for the expressive lines and the subject matter to speak evocatively. Burns’s monochromatic treatment of the paintings with its beautiful, sensitive lines made me think of some of M. C. Escher’s works. Roland Burns (1942-2024) was from New York City and won recognition for his supernatural, dream-like subject matter inspired by Surrealism. After studying at the School of Visual Arts, he relocated to Denmark in 1965, where he became associated with the artistic community centered around Galerie Passepartout, showcasing his unique talent through his distinct, symbolic paintings. Burns also made surrealistic paintings in oil such as “Floating Woman” (1967), which caught my attention with its unique blend of figure and seascape and its intriguing composition and use of negative space.

Walter Williams’s painting “Sunflowers” (1975-1976) is a unique work of art in the exhibition. Painted on a round canvas (diam. 25 7/8), the warm and intense hues of the subject matter (sunflowers, the sky and the sun) and the texture of the painting (oil and sand on Masonite) caught my eye. It made me think of the landscape as a visual manifestation of Williams’s energy and emotions. Walter Williams (1920-1998) was an artist from Brooklyn, NY, who traveled to Denmark in 1956, after receiving a John Hay Whitney Fellowship. Williams seemed to be always seeking opportunities, making art, and was prolific. From 1959 to 1963, he traveled and painted in Mexico and had exhibitions in venues such as the Instituto Nacional de Bellas Artes in Mexico City. Williams’s second wife was from Denmark, and in 1979 he became a Danish citizen, giving up his U.S. citizenship. In the foreground and middle ground of his painting “Southern Landscape” (1977-1978), black children pick cotton and sunflowers, while butterflies and birds fly overhead. The scenery looks dreamy and rustic, evoking a sense of tenderness of childhood in the mixed media painting (48 x 48). But looking at some of the visual references, such as cotton fields and a shanty made me wonder how free the children are. The foreground is beautifully detailed with flowers and grass, creating a sense of life and warmth.

Looking at the works of the three painters together in the exhibition, I thought about how the flowers and animals could represent forces of nature, vitality, lifecycle and change. And I thought about how we humans also share and possess such vitality and lifeforce. We may overcome obstacles, including problems that are structural. I thought about how the artists’ journeys in the Nordic countries may appear idyllic, and at the same time, when reflecting on the artists’ stories closely, I notice the complexities of their journeys. The energy of children and the vibrancy of flowers in Williams’s painting may convey a better future and possibilities for black Americans. In essays such as “Stranger in the Village,” James Baldwin expresses his frustration and ambivalent feelings towards Europe, while he also discusses the possibilities there, which were not available in America––the reality that made the young Baldwin decide to leave America for Paris as a writer. I thought about Baldwin’s writings, as I looked at the paintings in the exhibition and listened to the information shared during the tour. The title of the exhibition “Nordic Utopia?” reflects the ambiguous and complex realities of the artists seeking opportunities and inspiration in Scandinavia, where they hoped that race wouldn’t be an obstacle in seeking new possibilities. To answer whether or not this was the case is complicated. Thinking about the curatorial directions and the tour, I feel that while some of the artists felt frustration and held ambivalent feelings towards the Nordic societies, others also found personal happiness and occupational opportunities and successes––it appears mixed. 

As a teen, I was interested in Nordic design and music, and so, I thought about how the black American musicians toured and performed in the Nordic cities influencing the local music scenes. I thought about the impact the black painters had on the Nordic design scenes and art communities. It was mentioned during the tour that the jazz clubs became salons, where black artists gathered. The visitors of the tour were also reminded that while these artists were expats, many of the immigrants in Scandinavia coming from the Middle East and Africa didn’t have the same kinds of opportunities or experiences that the artists in the exhibition had. As Baldwin’s writings reflected the convoluted relationship he had with America and Europe, the artworks and documentary evidence in “Nordic Utopia?” suggest the mixed experiences of the artists and their varied views and stories in the Nordic countries. Viewers may reflect on the artists’ lives, as their sense of who they were was transformed through their experiences in Scandinavia. The paintings of Smith, Burns and Williams reveal their personal stories, and prompt viewers to think about questions of identity, migration, home, expatriation and immigration, and the artists’ journeys to find new possibilities in the Nordic countries.

A Personal Essay

By James Brooks

Last Spring, I joined a group of volunteers to replant native ʻaʻaliʻi and koaiʻa shrubs on the southern slope of Kohala Mountain on the Big Island, Hawai’i. At the Koaia Tree Sanctuary “we had a pretty good day,” said Jake Merkel of The Kohala Center. Planting around 100 “dibbles,” individual plantings, the hope is to re-establish the once-plentiful dry forests of the mountain. Drought tolerant and suited to this wind-swept area, these pleistocene megafauna were largely eradicated by the introduction of cattle grazing. 

Jake told us the replanting work would help mitigate erosion that occurs after heavy rains and allow other lower, native species to reestablish themselves. The now, mostly forest-less southern slope of the mountain, was accelerating runoff creating mudflows that were regularly inundating Kawaihae Bay. The mud covers “the coral, blocking out the sun and disrupts corral photosynthesis,” he said. Once each individual dibble was planted into the ground and quickly watered by another volunteer with a 5-gallon water tank strapped to their back, he told the group that it was “now part of your ʻohana’ (family).”

Before the United States supplanted it under duress, Hawaiian society prescribed different political identities to nature and to their individual selves. As Hawaiian language expert Mahina Patterson has said, Native Hawaiian cultural politics “associated patriotism with aloha a’ina (love of land).” This, in contrast to the U.S. American colonizers’ more solipsistic definitions where land exists mainly to serve it. A Hawaiian political identity was “he ali’i ka ʻāina, he kauā ke kanaka” — “the land is a chief and man is its servant and kama ‘aina; a man is a child of the land,” Patterson explained. 

Perhaps typical to many agrarian societies, Native Hawaiians assigned land and water with a clear power to give and take away life. The land took priority over the Hawaiian individual, who would typically introduce the ʻāina and wai,’ the land and body of water where they came from, before themselves in a social situation. Philosopher Celia Bardwell-Jones at the University of Hawaii, Hilo called this land-and-people organizing principle the opposite of a more anthropocentric, “Western environmental ethic that seeks to make nature more like us,” which “never made any sense.” “All of nature has standing” is the logical extension of its vitalizing power and said Bardswell-Jones, a Hawaiian political culture “already deduced personhood or rights” to all of nature. 

The “Hawaiian patriot,” Patterson explained, already saw “natural and cultural resources as one in the same.” With virtually no distinction between people, land or plant, mud suffocating coral in Kawaihae Bay would have been readily understood as a national affront. In pre-contact Hawaiian society there would have been no need for Western scientific concepts like “rewilding” that have evolved out of the increased urgency of climate change and the extinction crisis. The native dry forest already had rights which encompassed their practical ability to control erosion, which was explicitly threatening the coral, not to mention, the people who work at the Port of Kawaihae. I could feel proud to replant because it helped control erosion but also, because I owed it to my nation which already valued the pragmatic service of the dry forest. 

Proud because a restored watershed had the potential to help everyone attain a certain version of success, regardless of their social standing. Belonging to a nation that knows it depends on the flourishing of plants means patriots will more likely take selfless action to ensure this. Which meant a rigorous structure of interdependency would fall into place along with its obligatory demands. Social scientist Hugh Frazer wrote in “The Interdependence of Democracy and Social Cohesion” that in a functioning democracy, free people must actively identify the causes of disempowerment so that all individuals are participating in upholding the rights of others and the collective well-being. Holding this all together meant the patriot had to uncritically recognize the healthy freedoms of their sometimes illegible, social other. In an “inclusive participatory democracy,” the patriot could more easily feel blindly responsible for upholding these rights. 

If a nation was notoriously dependent on its patriots preserving the freedoms of enigmatic plants, patriots recognized, and were answerable to, the influence of koaiʻa and ʻaʻaliʻi and Kawaihae Bay coral. In this nation it is easier to see that people’s jobs at the Port of Kawaihae were dependent on their autonomy. Patriots had to share power with plants, but for me too, it was gratifying to protect the port from the mud by planting 17 inconspicuous dibbles that day. 

The port, the coral, and in turn, my satisfaction, also depended on obscure plants with their unique skill to reduce mudflow. A tenuous negotiation with plants so they could thrive was required. Non-negotiation in this nation too, was difficult to imagine. It didn’t include the erosion-controlling talents of plants, which happened to protect coral reefs that provide US$ 30 billion in net benefits in goods and services to world economies. Replanting dibbles was like working side-by-side within a community. I was trying to balance the value and the tensions between the long-term, simultaneous needs of the people, the dibbles, and the coral. Reconciling one competing freedom with another was hard but trying was a natural impulse where the Port of Kawaihae already needed plants. It felt righteous and industrious to fortify the watershed which was more like ensuring everyone had the freedom to assume their proper role in this nation. It was an even prouder accomplishment where everyone in this nation could be free to do this and when a patriot anticipated a tenuous coexistence with plants that had executive authority. Re-establishing compatriot relationships was a satisfying hole-digging, fertilizing, and watering procedure. 

The success of the reunion between three, often opposing factions could decide how muddy the port and bay are after a major rainfall. I was trying to achieve solidarity between quarrelsome family members and less mud was the disciplining factor. Making sure everyone got what they needed could be satisfying in part because it comes from knowing the port’s operations and the coral in the bay, would benefit only when the ʻaʻaliʻi and koaiʻa’ are thriving. But creating these “buffers” of zoned systems that include a functioning dry forest network along with, hopefully, a working Port of Kawaihae and breathing coral, would be the ceaseless work of conflict resolution. Stability would be determined by a tense, but advantageous relationship. I was not  “protecting” ecosystems, but trying to successfully traverse what plants and people wanted and needed. Lawrence Frank in his 1928 The Management of Tensions, called this trying to achieve “a general tensional adjustment.” By replanting native forests, a “semieffective substitute,” rewilding was the active achievement towards the remote goals of erosion control. The human need for the port, Frank called it the “exigencies of a social life,” demanded the full capabilities of plants making a functioning watershed. Ensuring everyone thrives was “learning tensional management.” The economic circumstances of the port required the ability to “sustain, diffuse, and defer the release of these tensions according to the tasks” of a more mud-stable mountainside dependent on a living forest. 

Mud-stability would help the coral photosynthesize and allow people to work. Replanting native species was the “active,” “mature” part of this tensional management which came with emotional stakes. Attempting to achieve good family relations is to know we are close but also to contend with our fraught differences. You managed the difference because your nation already assumed it would be difficult to negotiate with people whose agency could keep the port operating. If any part of the negotiation collapsed, you knew you would have to start over and somehow find agreement which further illustrates our dependency on each other. Because they knew they were dependent on the power of plants, the patriot would engage in a constructive conflict that saw all the different needs as the same and as assets, and the energy of conflict between them, an affirmation of our commitment to each other. Rewilding followed a kinship with nature model of constantly arousing and reaffirming an inescapably old and dedicated relationship. “Natural resource management” was not an intangible practice but an inherently complicated navigation of people’s differing expectations and personal vulnerability. It was the constant work of adjusting to everyone’s different needs and perspectives. 

Replanting––this was the rigorous Hālau ʻŌhiʻa’ or “kincentric” work of coordinating our differences, was rich nonetheless with notions of well-being. When my nation is universally empowered to think of its welfare as irreducibly dependent on receiving the benefits of all its citizens’ talents, keeping mud out of the bay can reward the patriot with lasting, positive emotional and physical advantages. Understanding that freedom means reckoning with interdependencies well is “optimal learning” critical to health, said Noelani Goodyear-Kaʻōpua of the University of Hawaii, Manoa. Jake, who had over the years consistently showed up to the mountain with his truck and planted Ōhi’a, Koai’a, and ʻA’ali’i, helped establish a protective dry forest on the upper slope of the Koaia Sanctuary. Now a ubiquitous part of the landscape, his pride was obvious. After the planting that day he said, “let’s hope for a good rain afterward,” and when it did rain the very next day, I rushed up to the mountain to check on my seedlings. Standing there in the rain, if I could help plants be plants I could keep mud out of Kawaihae Bay. I felt good because I knew life was going to be a little better for everyone.
