By Meg Kaizu

I follow Bella in the woods. We are 11. She is walking with her camera in her hands. It’s the middle of the summer. She is dressed in green, blending into the lush background of the Alps. Her soft curly hair is braided and pinned. In the sun she looks frail as though a spirit. She turns around and says, “Nadia, you are so slow! I’ll leave you here.” She’s no spirit, I think to myself, as I hear her loud yell.

“Stop yelling! Calm down,” I stick my tongue out.

“These butterflies are pretty. I don’t want to miss them,” Bella points at them in the trees.

“I think there are too many of them today. Like they are waiting for something.”

“Waiting for what?” 

“I don’t know…” I see her face cloud.

The phone rang in my apartment in Milan. I answered and heard my mother’s sad voice. “Nadia, I am wondering if you can come home and help me around the house.”

“I’m always here to help. Don’t worry,” I said with a smile in an attempt to appease her. 

“It’s been lonely here, ever since your father died.” 

“How have you been feeling?”

“I’ve been taking sleeping pills. I have horrifying nightmares.” Her voice broke. I packed my things and left for my hometown the following week. I told my boyfriend Rhigi that I would be back in a few weeks.

As I boarded the train, Righi said, “Don’t get too comfortable in the Alps. I’m waiting for you here in Milan. And don’t forget your camera. Here.” 

I turned around and said, “I will be back soon. Can you keep my camera? I don’t think I’ll need it over there.” 

The sky was dry and blue, until it suddenly started raining.

I sat in the train and pictured Bella, as the landscape of the Alps flew by outside the window. She was a lively, spirited girl. She had long flowing hair that came down to her waist, freckles on her nose and brown eyes. Wind carrying a scent of grass made me long for home. For a moment I wished I had brought the camera with me, but soon I reconciled thinking it’s better to remember things as they are. Over the years, my memory of Bella faded, replaced by somewhat never-ending concerns of everyday life. Remembering her was painful for the most part. I could never imagine Bella growing older. While I finished school and moved to Milan for college, Bella did none of these things, as she went missing and was never found. I kept in contact with her family for a long time, even after they left Italy. Eventually I left my hometown for college and lost touch with them. The fall of the Berlin Wall and the collapse of the Soviet Union left virtually no effect on our Italian village in the Alps. The world moved on without Bella. 

On the night I arrived home, I called Righi. “My mom is feeling better. She says she is not as disturbed as she was, you know, before I came home.”

“That’s great. Keep her happy, Nadia. Be a good daughter. It’s hard to be widowed. And she’s lonely in the village.”

“Oh, I will be good. Well, I need to go. It’s time for me to go to sleep.” 

“Hey, I just wanted to tell you. You know the film you left? After it was developed, I looked at the photos and found something strange.”

“What do you mean strange?”

“I’ll show you when you come back. Anyhow, go to sleep. Talk to you tomorrow, okay?”  

I agreed to call him tomorrow and put down the phone. I went downstairs and made sure my mother was asleep. When I came back to my room, I turned off the light and laid down in my bed. I looked at the wall in the dim distance. The moonlight came in from the window. Silence filled the room. Bella was standing by the window in the moonlight. 

“I’ve been waiting for you.”

“What do you mean?” I rubbed my eyes and looked around. She was no longer there. I wasn’t sure if I were dreaming. It felt as if she came to visit me from somewhere.

Bella walks before me in the field. The sun is bright. She follows and takes pictures of butterflies with the camera her grandfather has given her. The color of their wings is vivid. Bella is good at capturing the hue, under the right condition for photography, creating an intriguing atmosphere. She could narrate stories through imagery. She sits in the darkroom with her mother and develops her films all evening. When she is there, she does not come out to play with me. 

“You can come into the room and see the pictures.” 

“It’s creepy in there. So dark and cold and smells funny.” 

“You get scared easily,” she looks at me, amused. 

She runs around in her summer dress and takes photographs in the fields, woods, near the stone houses. What is she looking for? 

“Let’s go take pictures in that stone house,” Bella says. 

“That place creeps me out. Don’t you remember the story our grandparents told us? People died from the plague in there.”

“Don’t be silly! People die everywhere. I’m sure people died in your house, too.”

“Stop! I won’t be able to sleep tonight.”

Bella and I spent a lot of time together as children. But after having lived in Milan, I began to feel like it was never part of my life. I started to forget a lot about my childhood and Bella. I sat near the apple tree in my mother’s backyard and looked at the mountains. They were as lush as I remembered them to be. My mother cut vegetables in the kitchen. There was a smell of dinner. I got up, started picking apples on the ground and carefully put them in a basket. I pictured Bella. She smiled in her yellow dress with sunflowers on it. She hummed and chuckled. Butterflies flew in the view – the type of image Bella would have captured in her picture.

At dinner I said to my mother, “I started seeing a lot of butterflies in the village, since I returned from Milan.” 

“Oh yes? I haven’t noticed anything.”

I fell silent. Butterflies had disappeared from the village, since Bella went missing. I always felt like butterflies had no reason to live here, since Bella was not looking for them. 

“Do you want more wine?” my mother asked.

“No, it’s okay.” I got up and started washing the dishes. “I’m tired. We should go to sleep.”

Bella is in the green dress. It’s pretty on her. The sun is bright. She leads the way. We need to find butterflies. It’s hard to keep up with her. She walks fast. I’m thirsty. Can we go home? She says no. It’s getting late. The sun will set soon. Let’s go home.

I go to Bella’s house. “Mrs. Visconte, did Bella come home?” 

“No, since she left with you this morning, she hasn’t come back.” 

“Bella went to take pictures. She was looking for butterflies.”

“You know, she does that sometimes. She does whatever she wants. No need to worry. You’ll be the first person to know when she comes home.”

Bella never came home that night. By 10 PM, her family knew something had happened and that Bella was not coming home. 

“You know I’ve been looking at these albums,” my mother said, turning the pages. “The pictures your father took.”

“How come?” 

“I miss him. But I want to stop being sad.”

My mother and I were clearing the shelf. It smelled dusty in the living room.

“You shouldn’t force anything.” 

“It’s nice to see what he was seeing, you know, through the pictures.” 

I watched tears form in her eyes. 

“It’s almost like seeing through his eyes.” She gazed out the window. 

I sat by my desk and looked at the photographs Bella gave me. Among them was a portrait of me. “It’s almost like seeing through his eyes…” What did my father see? What did Bella see? I looked at the picture of myself. My stone house and apple trees were captured in the background. What did Bella find through the lens? When I photographed, I wasn’t sure. It was tiring. As a photographer for my friend’s wedding, I wondered if the pictures were real. Why do people want to keep images? That afternoon when I asked Bella to call it a day, she looked me in the eye and said, “You are just scared. I’m going alone.” 

“I dreamt about Bella last night,” I said to Righi over the phone.

“Did she say anything in the dream?”

“She was angry and said I’m a coward.”

“Come on, Nadia. Spending too much time with the villagers is not good for you. And there’s nothing to do in the countryside.”

“I feel more and more depressed. I can’t think clearly…” I put away Bella’s photographs in the drawer, “I should come back to Milan and move on with my life.”

I bought my train ticket after the phone conversation but didn’t tell my mother about it. She might get upset about my departure. I cleaned my room, cleared things in the chest and found a letter that I never sent to Bella’s mother.

Dear Mrs. Visconte, 

I am sorry I have not written to you for a long time. I hope you are well in New York. As for me, I’m enrolled in college full-time, and work when I’m not in class. I’ve taken a few photography classes, thinking of majoring in it. I wish Bella could have taken these classes with me. I’m sure she would have loved them. Bella was my closest friend and I miss her dearly. 

I look forward to your letter.

Sincerely,

Nadia

The silver moonlight poured through the window. I was increasingly aware of sounds in the house. Something moved. I used every nerve in my body to sense any presence around me. Butterflies flew in the moonlit room. Bella was sitting on my chair.

She spoke softly, “Do you remember the river?” 

“Of course I do. We used to play there.” 

“I’ve been waiting for you there.”

“Since when?”

In the dark I traced the path we took, just as I followed her in the daylight that day. The smell of wet mud filled the air. Butterflies were everywhere around me. The body of a girl floated in the water. She wore the bead bracelet I gave to Bella for her 11th birthday. The soft brown hair clung to her arms. Tears streamed down my cheeks. “I know…I remember…” I whispered under my breath and held her body in my arms. Bella’s scream echoed.

“I’m sorry I didn’t find you earlier…” I carried her out of the dark water. The butterflies flew circling above us, muffling all the sounds in the valley.

By David O. Monda

Donald Trump came into office after his January 20th inauguration as a man on a mission. His plans for this second term were clearly spelt out in his campaign rhetoric and manifesto. A center of his campaign was getting tough on immigration. He has quickly backed his words with action. Three of his main actions on immigration have been cancelling birthright citizenship – the right of anyone born in the U.S. to automatically gain U.S. citizenship, passing the Laken Riley Act through Congress and declaring a state of emergency at the southern border with Mexico. This combination of anti-immigrant measures is central to why Trump’s second term makes life even harder for Africans without documents in the USA.

According to the Pew Research Center, there are 11 million undocumented immigrants in the USA. Of these, approximately two million are from Sub Saharan Africa. Trump’s Executive Order eliminating birthright citizenship to the children of undocumented immigrants further marginalizes Africans without proper immigration documentation. While 17 states have challenged the Trump Executive Order in court, it creates uncertainty and anxiety in immigrant communities. In the interim, the fate of children of undocumented immigrants and their families remains grim.

The passage of the Laken Riley Act also shrinks the legal protections for undocumented immigrants. It allows state and federal authorities expanded leeway to deport undocumented immigrants convicted of theft related crimes. This action effectively lowers the threshold for the severity of crimes for which individuals can get deported. While under the Biden Administration, the focus was on undocumented immigrants that committed felonies, simple misdemeanors could land an undocumented immigrant in line for deportation.

What is more troubling with the Laken Riley Act is the expanded role of the states in implementing federal immigration policy. Border regulation and immigration policy has heretofore been domiciled with the federal government in Washington D.C and not the states. It is an enumerated constitutional power of the federal government to regulate the border and advance immigration policy. Not the states. We should be even more disturbed by the perverse incentives created by the Laken Riley Act. Because the Trump Administration will need an additional 60,000 beds to detain undocumented immigrants, at a cost of approximately $3 billion, local and state governments are further incentivized to rent detention capacity for the undocumented immigrants to the federal government via the Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE). This practice disproportionately targets vulnerable migrant populations (mainly people from poor developing regions like Africa) that have limited access to legal support and are faced with wider environmental and societal marginalization.

Lastly, in declaring a state of emergency at the southern border with Mexico and militarizing the border region with additional troops, Trump has made it more difficult for asylum seekers attempting to cross the border to save their lives. The crisis at the U.S.-Mexico border has resulted in thousands of asylum seekers stuck in Mexico in unhygienic, dangerous, and destitute conditions with no quick way to file an asylum claim or petition to enter the U.S. In addition to this, the legal process of applying for visas to the U.S. takes many months, if not years. This totality of anti-immigrant Trump-led federal policy therefore makes life even harder for Africans without documents in the USA. It is incumbent upon the African Union and individual African governments to push back on Trump’s xenophobic immigrant policies or risk further marginalizing undocumented Africans––an already vulnerable migrant population––in the USA.

By Meg Kaizu

 

 

On the first night in Newnan, I walk downtown to see the antebellum houses. I take pictures of them and send them to my family: “I’m in Georgia for my artist residency!” When I get to the square, a man on a bench asks me where I’m from. “I came from New York,” I answer. He says, “I mean which country are you from?” “I’m from Japan.” He tells me, or asks me about China’s censorship of Facebook. A woman next to him says China doesn’t allow people to use Facebook. I say, “I heard use of some websites is restricted but people find ways to visit them.” The man says, “Well, it’s like here, you can’t drink until 21, but people find ways anyways.” I cross the street, walk toward the courthouse and find a memorial about William Thomas Overby, a Confederate soldier. It says he was “the Nathan Hale of Confederacy” and “suffered death rather than betray his friends.”

On the following day, I return to the square and walk into a visitor center. I look at numerous brochures about Newnan, antebellum houses, the Battle of Brown’s Mill, the Atlanta Campaign, Gone with the Wind, the Trail of Tears, Murder in Coweta County and so on. A Black man with a cane walks into the room and talks to a clerk about the history of Newnan. I run into him again outside the courthouse. He asks me if I’m Japanese or Korean. I say I’m Japanese. He tells me he is an ethnologist and studies various cultures. “I studied about your culture, too. Do you know about the indigenous people in Japan?” I say, “There were a few waves of migrations into the archipelago.” “The indigenous people came from Africa,” he says. He looks up at the statue on the square and says, “People don’t know what it means.” I say, “Yes, I looked at the memorials on the square, about Confederacy.” He tells me about his work, his faith, says we had a conversation for a reason. He gives me a business card and tells me he and his wife can come pick me up to go to church on Sunday. “You should walk into a church downtown and think about Christ.”

I walk into a restaurant called Golden’s, pick up a local magazine and find an article about the best restaurants to get biscuits and gravy in the region. I circle the names of the restaurants in Newnan. When people see me paint the courthouse, they stop and make comments. A woman yells at me from her car window, “What are you painting?” I show her my watercolor. She says, “It’s good.” Another woman approaches me with a smile and says she likes my painting. Cathy says she’s an art teacher, and asks if I want to come join her class. I get up and follow her to an art gallery.

Another memorial on the square says Coweta County was created by Creek cessions of 1826. “It was named Coweta to perpetuate the fame of the head chief of the Coweta Towns, General William McIntosh, half-blood Creek Indian. Gen. McIntosh, daring soldier and useful ally during the War with the British, was killed in his home by some of his own people after he signed the Treaty at Indian Springs, ceding land to the Whites.”

In Mary Beth’s writing, I find that by 1910, a local newspaper reported that Newnan was the fourth-wealthiest town per capita in the United States. She writes, “Speaking of his ancestors’ contribution to the town’s white ruling class, one black man told me, ‘I earned that money for them, and I didn’t get anything.’”

“People are nice to you if you are white,” Jonas said before I left for Atlanta, speaking of Southern hospitality. He has visited North Carolina and Alabama as a journalist. I wasn’t sure if he was making a matter-of-fact statement or warning me. I recalled my roommate Michelle in Tennessee. When I visited her home and showed her family some pictures from Japan, her father said, “You have a temple made of gold in Japan? If it were in America, somebody would steal it.” I forgot to mention Kinkaku-ji was burnt down by a monk. Now it’s re-built and looks shiny.

People are nice, and as I paint, I wonder what being a nice person means. I can be nice and still hold prejudices. We can all have good intentions but that may not be enough. Justin said we have blind spots. Maybe our being nice is not complete: a work in progress. Maybe we have to expand our moral imagination, as Richard Wright said.

“Our Confederate dead, whom power could not corrupt, whom death could not terrify, whom defeat could not dishonor. It is not in mortals to command success. But they did more – deserved it. 1861-1865.” The passage is inscribed on a base on the square, on which a uniformed Confederate soldier stands on picket duty.

In the art gallery, Cathy and her student say, “You’re only here for 2 weeks?” I say I wish I could stay here longer. We talk about antebellum houses, largely untouched by the Civil War due to Newnan’s status as a hospital city. I was excited about painting them before I came to Georgia.

I ride the bike to the African American Heritage Museum. On the way I see a mill and the railroad. I take pictures and cross the railway. On the other side, I see old houses, some of which have broken windows. I wonder if it is a poorer part of the city. NYC has poor neighborhoods and a large homeless population with its overwhelming income gap. People look at me, wonder who I am. I say hi. When I see a pond, I walk up to take pictures. Quickly, a snake slithers into the pond. I shriek.

On Greenville Street, I photograph antebellum houses, cross the railroad, and ride my bicycle along Martin Luther King Jr. Bulverde. People look at me. I make a turn and keep biking. I see a sign: “Housing Authority.” The following day, I find an article about a shooting: “A Newnan resident has been charged in the April 4 shooting death of a Newnan man on Octavia Place.” I was there, I think to myself.

I keep talking about biscuits and gravy since my arrival in Newnan. When people recommend restaurants to me, I take notes. At Christy’s I tell a waitress, “When I studied in Tennessee, I had biscuits and gravy every morning. Do you serve white gravy?” She says they do. I recall the hills, the thunderstorms I watched from my window in Tennessee, and the sun shining over rain-soaked grass. When she brings the dish, I see a plate full of biscuits and gravy, fried eggs and a sausage patty.

In the Carnegie Library’s meeting room, I greet people and sit down to talk about my background and experience as a writer and painter. Cathy asks me how I am. I say I’m a bit tired. I don’t mention the poor neighborhood, projects. I am starting to feel weary, isolated, disoriented. I appreciate everything that’s been done for me. We are all nice, but that doesn’t make inequality or poverty go away. As I take questions, a woman asks if I write haiku. She says her husband is Japanese. “I don’t personally write haiku, but some American authors like Richard Wright and Sonia Sanchez have written them.”

At the Oak Hill Cemetery, I see a Confederate flag, which overlooks the confederate soldiers’ graves. The sign says, “269 Confederate soldiers and 2 Revolutionary War soldiers are buried here.” I look up at the flag again.

At McRichie-Hollis Museum, I pick up a book of paper dolls of Southern belles in the gift shop. Two young ladies can be dressed in fashionable ball dresses. Each dress comes with detailed descriptions of the time, vogue and story. The women are escorted by a young man, who can be dressed in a Confederate uniform. The book describes Southern plantation owners as American kings and queens.

I’m boiling rice and slices of bananas in whole milk, and add salt and cinnamon. I keep boiling them but the rice doesn’t steam. I stay up late to finish making the dish. By the morning, it’s soft and sweet and tasty.

I watched Gone with the Wind with my boss’s sister Annie and their mother in Haines, Alaska. Mimi had dementia and asked who I was many times. She and I finished watching the movie together. I thought of what my mother told me: my grandmother saw the movie after the war and said, “Why did Japan go to war with the U.S.? It was clear Japan wouldn’t win. The U.S. was a country that could produce a movie like that.”

When I learned new words in Tennessee, I took notes: slavery, half-breed, thirteen colonies and so on. I had to rely on a dictionary and explanations teachers gave and guess a lot then, and after all these years I still guess. I learn new words like carpetbagger and Southern belle in Newnan. Cathy and Lynn are Yankees.

Dolly shows me the slave burial ground at the African American Heritage Museum, the biggest in the South. She points at a few private houses that stand on a part of the burial ground today. If that portion of the cemetery is officially recognized, she says, “It will beat the one in NYC.” When I go inside the museum, she shows me a photograph of Martin Luther King Jr.’s brother in Newnan. He was a preacher at one of the churches in town. When another staff member comes in, they start talking about a rally. I ask, “What rally?” It’s the neo-Nazi rally.” “Is it the group that went to Charlottesville last summer?” “Same people!”

With board members from the residency, I am eating fried pickles, looking at a menu at a restaurant downtown. Briana recommends me to try shrimp and grits and fried green tomato salad. I order them. Lynn tells us about her half-Japanese, half-Jewish nephew. His father was born in the internment camp in California. “You might be interested in learning more about this, too.” I say I am.

 

In his article “Japanese American authors expand frame in works on WWII internee kin”, Justin writes, “Yamashita explained that she was writing toward ‘some kind of reconciliation,’ but noted the recent rise of nativism in U.S. politics has made the fight against racism and anti-immigrant policies as demanding as ever.” Yamashita said, “I want everybody to read everything they can read and put their bodies in front of what is going on.”

Briana says, “It’s awful that these things happened to Japanese-Americans.” Lynn says, “Oh, it can happen now. In fact, the neo-Nazi rally will be held here on April 21st.” I mention I heard about the rally at the African American Heritage Museum and that churches are holding services on the day in response to the rally. “It has to be more than a Christian response. Muslims, Jews and other people have to be there, too,” Lynn says. We talk about the National Socialist Movement, a neo-Nazi political party based in Detroit. Briana looks at me and says, “Southern whites must oppose it. Everyone must oppose it. I hope this serves as a wake-up call among Southerners. Southern belles care about social conscience.”

I’m reading the article “10 things to know about the upcoming white-supremacist rally” in Newnan Times-Herald:

Dolly says, “Schools were segregated. And I started school in 1970, a few years after the school segregation ended. My boyfriend in second grade was black. There were segregated counties in New York, too.” I say, “I’m not surprised. My friend told me public schools in NYC are very segregated. I read articles about that.” Things change; nothing remains the same. But things are not changing fast enough.

Many of my students in the Bronx are Black and Hispanic. Many speak Spanish, from whom I learned some Spanish words. They’ve asked or made comments or jokes about race or racism, about “getting deported,” “selling and buying people”.

I walk into Super Latino and look for flour, baking powder, cheese and pasta. People speak in Spanish. Some products have labels only in Spanish. I wish I knew the language better, after having taken two classes. I think of saying something in Spanish, but just smile at a clerk and say, “Gracias,” as she hands me my groceries.

I re-look at my painting of the University of West Georgia. It’s not coming out right. I remember David Boyd Jr.’s landscape paintings in his gallery downtown. A few of them are architectural paintings and very beautiful. At his first Friday painting demonstration, David mentioned he wished to focus on architecture, cityscape and figures in the future. I start painting the University mechanically. It’s difficult to deal with a lot of plain, horizontal, vertical lines. In the email, my teacher says I did very well with the architectural paintings, saying it’s a difficult subject for him to paint, too, because it has no rhythm. It is all geometric forms, boxes, cylinders, verticals, horizontals, and there is no light that makes it look more interesting. Painting Lynn’s pond on her property brings back a sense of joy, as it feels familiar, comforting. “Painting landscape is easier,” I tell her. “Painting architecture is not. I abstract some elements in painting, but with architecture it’s hard. People won’t notice a few trees missing, but they will notice missing windows.” Slowly, I learn to abstract architecture. Strong light and shadow help create depth and contrast. I’m eating lunch at Golden’s when Taylor from The Newnan Times-Herald calls me. I give an interview over the phone and answer Taylor’s questions, as she is in Atlanta. Briana arranged it for me, so Taylor can write an article about me for the town paper. I wish I were a better speaker. I’m afraid of misphrasing, saying wrong things, being misunderstood. Maybe I write and paint because I’m mad, but I better have more enticing answers.

I write to Josh in Birmingham: “It’s hard for me to get a sense of this community. The town has Confederate memorials and graves, which are considered heritage, and which partly attracted the National Socialist Movement to come rally. To write about this is to write about America and its history. It’s very challenging.”

Cathy takes me to Moreland, and I meet her friend Dan, his wife and their son. As I chat with Dan, I say I am writing about the neo-Nazi rally. “I was wondering if people are used to getting this type of group rallying in Newnan.” Dan says it’s very unusual, “Many people were deported during the Obama administration, too. I’m for open borders. I think people can come and go, as they wish.” He smiles. Outside their house, I take pictures of their dog and cat, their house, art studio, and old barn. On our way back to Newnan, Cathy and I see cars escorted by a police car. “It’s a funeral,” she says and pulls over. “People don’t do it as much in the North.”

I’m reading an interview with Joanna Schoep, who was married to Jeff Schoep, the “commander” of the National Socialist Movement. She calls the organization a political cult:

“I went to rallies with Jeff, and his followers just worship him. No one can question Jeff. Everybody called him ‘commander.’ No one could differ with him.” 

“I consider them his ‘followers’ because it is a cult, and a big one. Jeff’s main focus is getting as much money from people as possible. Even though he says it’s not.”

The Newnan Times-Herald quotes Martin Luther King Jr. in an article “50 years later: Cowetans Reflect on King’s Legacy:” “What is needed is a realization that power without love is reckless and abusive, and love without power is sentimental and anemic. Power at its best is love, implementing the demands of justice, and justice at its best is love correcting everything that stands against love.”

TAYLOR BRANCH: The Movement took a huge toll on him. When they did the autopsy, they said he had the heart of a 60 year old, he’s 39. So yes, it took a big toll on him, and he was constantly fantasizing about getting out of the Movement, but I don’t know of anybody around him who ever took it seriously, who felt that even he really thought that he could follow through on that. The Movement was his life.

Anna texts me and asks how things are, “I heard Georgia is weird.” I shrug and think to myself, “Well, Oregon is weird, too.” I’ve told her some people in New York called Pacific Northwesterners passive-aggressive PC people. New York is weird. Japan is weird. When I tell her about Confederate memorials, graves and flags, she replies, “Oh man! That’s intense. I guess it’s that I’ve heard repeatedly that the South feels like a different country, kind of stuck in the past.”

I write to Justin, “I’m getting homesick, or the excitement is wearing off. As an outsider, I’m always testing the water, learning and getting confused. But this is true in NYC, and in the wider world. Life is not there to guarantee safety, security, etc.”

I go back to Super Latino to get shrimp and sausages. A clerk asks me what I’m looking for. I tell him I want to make shrimp and grits and ask him how much the shrimp cost. As we converse, I ask, “Are there many Hispanic people in Newnan?” “Well, used to. Not so many, any more. You know, it’s hard to work here these days. But I hope they will come back, because we need people.” He smiles.

I am painting one of the College Temple buildings built in 1856. I have frequented the site, and some residents remember me. A woman approaches me, looks at my painting and smiles. “It’s nice.” She says her daughter Hannah volunteers at Backstreet Art. “Do you know about the place? They have classes and art supplies for people who can’t afford them.” I say, “I’ve heard about them, and I’ve wanted to go.” When Hannah gets home, she comes to talk to me. She says she will be at Backstreet Art in the evening.

I write to Helen in New York, “Over here, townspeople have been talking about a neo-Nazi rally scheduled in a few weeks. I’m going to the city council’s meeting this afternoon. I’ve been thinking about it and writing about it, which is disheartening. Apart from the project, I’ve been plein air painting, taking some photographs, making collages, writing poems, etc.”

I ride my bicycle to Backstreet Art. Hannah shows me around the studio and hands me fluid art supplies. I’ve never tried it before. For 30 minutes, I watch how paints move across the canvas. Hannah smiles and says it’s therapeutic to her. It’s true. When I come home, I feel better. I sit down and write, trying to find words without sentimentalizing.

I fry shrimp in the pan. When they turn pink and crispy I take it off the stove. I couldn’t find grits in Super Latino so I use quinoa. Shrimp and quinoa taste delicious. When I make biscuits and gravy with chorizo sausages, I add flour and milk too early, and the whole gravy turns into a hamburg-steak-like mess.

In Newnan City Hall, people come up to the microphone and voice their concerns over the rally. A woman speaks of her worries about the safety of her community, her disabled mother, asks if it’s possible to quickly drive out to another town to care for her sick relative, if necessary. A man expresses concerns about safety and asks the City to provide security to the African American Heritage Museum. A woman asks about freedom of speech in relation to the hate group rally. Another woman asks why the city granted a permit to the National Socialist Movement and if they can’t revoke it.

I ride my bicycle in the Oak Hill Cemetery to find a good spot to paint. The view is pretty, peaceful and quiet. I pass all the beautiful gravestones and sculptures; I just want to paint cedars and oaks. I sit on the ground, set up my easel, and smell the dry grass. When I come home, I hang my paintings and pin the photographs on the wall, and finish writing.

At my open studio, I talk with guests about my experience as an artist-in-residence in Newnan, about the rally. I read my piece about my days in town. When Melissa asks what I thought about the Confederate memorials, I say I was shocked. She says she was brought up to think they were Southern heritage, “I have mixed feelings.” I talk about Columbus Circle, the Columbus statue and other monuments in NYC. Cathy says she wasn’t allowed to play with her black girlfriend in Pennsylvania. Briana says she noticed anti-Black sentiment among the Japanese when she went to stay with her son stationed in the U.S. naval base in Yokosuka. “The Black soldiers were discriminated against by white gaijin and the locals.”

Outside the Oak Hill Cemetery, I see a couple with signs: “Love Not Hate.” They say they grew up in Newnan and wanted to show they don’t approve of the neo-Nazi rally. I ask what they think of the Confederate memorials. “We never read them. They are part of the landscape. Nobody has said anything.” I thank them, wish them good luck, walk to McRichie-Hollis Museum and see a counter-demonstration across the street. A young man from Atlanta tells me, “This happens a lot in Atlanta but it’s unusual in a small town like this.” As we converse, we see SWAT arrest a protester. He says, “Protesters are not allowed to wear masks. That’s why they are getting arrested.” People take pictures and videos. I overhear there’s a legal team watching law enforcement, so they can report any legal issues with them. Near Greenville Street Park, more counter-demonstrators get arrested. One of the arrested men refuses to walk, and two policemen grab his arms and carry him. “You’re the real fascists!” somebody yells at the law enforcement. “They arrest white people, too,” a Black man says.

I sit on a brick flowerbed. A black man comes to sit down near me and we converse. He gives me and other people roses at the demonstration. He asks me if the hate group is here. I tell him they haven’t arrived. He says, “Main audience is not here.” I say, “Maybe they’re not coming.” I keep the rose to take home.

Across from the courthouse, I see a little girl with a chalk, drawing and writing words on the street. The police have left the square, and the tension has dissipated. Her mother is speaking to a camera in Spanish. She must be a journalist reporting on the rally. I take pictures of the little girl, and others. A young Black man writes, “Black love matters and cures White hate.” I talk to the journalist, who says when she spoke to Hispanic residents in Newnan, they were apprehensive about coming out to counter-demonstrate. They said the Hispanic community is small and the Black community has more visibility. I tell her Super Latino is right across from the Greenville Park. “I’m sure they are closed today,” I say. We talk about her work, about Atlanta, about her daughter accompanying her for the first time. I ask her for her business card. “Let’s stay in touch and meet in NYC.”

I’m sitting on a bench near the square, when a woman pulls over and gets out of her car. She says she was in Atlanta for a funeral and missed the rally, “I don’t get why people hate others because of color of skin. And I don’t get why they wanna show it.” Vicky says she didn’t experience racism back in Texas, adding, “When I got older, I saw it. I look white but I’m Black. I’m mixed.” She describes one of her sisters looks Hispanic, and the other looks Indian. “My sister was in a park, and some guy looked at her, and his wife got upset and called her the N-word. I would’ve wanted to be there.” We walk around the square and take pictures of messages people wrote on the streets the night before. Vicky says the statue needs to come down.

Near McRichie-Hollis Museum, a Lyft driver Cheryl picks me up. I’m grateful she found me. It’s late at night and my phone just died. I couldn’t reach her. As we leave a gas station, she asks, “Were you downtown today?” looking at me from the corner of her eye.

“Yes,” I answer. “I didn’t see the neo-Nazi rally but saw counter-protesters getting arrested.”

“Oh yes, police arrest people who are counter-protesting. Not the neo-Nazis.”

“I’m not from Georgia so I was surprised when I saw the Confederate memorials.”

“It’s not okay that the city is hosting this rally. I’m a Black American, and this is not okay. When people show off Confederate flags on their private property, it’s okay.”

“Is it okay?”

“What can you do? It’s private property. But when it’s public, it’s a different story. I am thinking of moving out of Newnan after this. You allow this once, and you will allow this again. People who have the feelings and sentiments will feel encouraged. That’s what’s scary. I don’t know if I’d last for another 2 years in Newnan, until my son graduates from school. You know you make sacrifices for your kid. The school is here, so I stay. White Americans are not hurt so they don’t see it. They can say Confederate memorials are just there.”

I say the conversations need to be centered around people who are affected. Cheryl says several people, White, Indian and Black, whom she gave rides to, said they consider leaving the town after this rally.

When we arrive at my host’s house, I thank Cheryl for the ride and get out of her car. She gives me her phone number just in case something happens in a place I don’t know.

In Atlanta, I visit the Martin Luther King Jr. National Historical Park and see videos of Whites in Chicago cursing at King, Freedom Riders, their bus being bombed, people opposing desegregation, about lynching, lynched victims, about King’s arrest. I pick up a book of photographs taken by Charles Moore. Children’s Crusade in Birmingham. I put it down, walk around Sweet Auburn and see King’s birth home and shotgun houses on Auburn Avenue. I read what’s written on each memorial. In the approaching thunderstorm, I run to the subway station. On my phone, I read about the National Socialist Movement’s swastika-burning in Draketown after the rally.

When the bus reaches NYC, it drives around lower Manhattan. A Black woman asks the Chinese bus driver to let her get off. “I need to go. My child is waiting.” The driver tells her to sit down. She refuses. They get into an argument. He calls her a bitch. As the bus approaches the bus stop in Chinatown, the Black woman calls him an animal, alien, a restart. A little girl watches them. When the bus stops, the little girl gets up and holds her mother’s hand. They speak in Spanish. I tell her to go ahead. After you. The little girl smiles. I get off the bus and run to make it to my class. When my students come into the classroom, some of them give me a hug and say they missed me. “Where were you, sensei?”

By Aida Lynn Eloumri

In August 2023, I was eagerly waiting on line at New York’s Moynihan Train Hall to board my Amtrak 137 Northeast Regional train for Washington D.C. After a long day of work and twenty minutes of waiting on line, I get hit with the worst news that no traveler wants to hear; “Ladies and Gentlemen, we are currently experiencing delays with all southbound trains heading for Penn Station.” I rolled my eyes in disgust and dropped my bag on the floor at the incompetence that is Amtrak. Meanwhile, I can hear the sucking of teeth, the moaning and the groaning, the huffing and puffing as customers vent out their frustration due to the subpar service. 

Amtrak was created after the passage of the Rail Passenger Service Act of 1970, which allowed the company to be incorporated. The company has the obligation of providing passenger rail service along with allowing private companies (mostly freight operators) to use their train tracks for private purposes. Since its inception, we have seen how Amtrak has been pushed aside by corporate freight companies who prioritize profits over passengers. Last summer, the United States District Court for the District of Columbia filed a complaint against Norfolk Southern Corporation and Norfolk Southern Railway Company due to the amount of delays they have caused on Amtrak’s tracks. The Crescent 19 and the Crescent 20 lines have felt the most impact by the delays caused by Norfolk Southern; with only 24% of trains arriving on time on the Crescent 19 line and only 48% of Crescent 20 trains arriving on time between 2022 and 2023.  What adds fuel to fire is knowing that over 70% of Amtrak’s travel is operated on train tracks owned by freight companies . It is absurd knowing Amtrak does not even have majority control over the tracks they operate on; it is like living in a run down apartment building and being at the mercy of your unreliable superintendent to fix the broken sink faucet. 

When we look at how Amtrak operates here in the U.S, it is a joke in comparison to our European counterparts. For example, France ( known for having the fifth fastest train in the world), has one of the most developed railway systems globally. SNCF (Société nationale des chemins de fer français) is a railway company that is fully owned by the French government and has rights and ownership over all of its train tracks that it operates on. On the other hand, we have Amtrak who only own 3% of the train tracks it operates its trains on while the remaining tracks are owned by private freight companies. Aside from track ownership, SNCF trains in 2023 only reported only 16% of TGV (Train à Grande Vitesse) trains were delayed, whereas Amtrak reported that only 56% of all of its long distance carrier trains arrived on time in 2023. 

Back in March 2024, I had the privilege of riding the TGV trains between Marseille, Lyon and Paris. From the active communication between announcers and passengers on train departure time, to the punctuality of arriving at every station on time without delay, as a train enthusiast, I was in train heaven questioning why this is not the norm for Amtrak. I have been a loyal customer to this company since 2022, using their service to travel through the Northeast Corridor. Every time I use their service, it is the same old song over and over again, no one telling us why we are delayed and I never arrive at my final destination on time. 

Being at the mercy of any private corporation to get anything done can be an uncomfortable position to be in. However, in 1980, Congress passed a bill called the Staggers Act, which deregulated the rail industry and allowed corporations to invest money into fixing the railroads. Shocking how a congressional bill that was passed during an era of deregulation ended up impacting those who will experience actual train delays, thanks a lot by way Congress.  

Like we see in France, where they have full ownership over the train tracks, we need to see Amtrak and the Department of Transportation stand up to private freight companies and take full ownership over the tracks they operate on. With the proper ownership and regulation of how private freight trains operate on their tracks, I can finally fulfill my lifelong dream of having Amtrak arriving at Moynihan Train Hall and to my final destination on time.

By Aida Lynn Eloumri

All aboard, as the biggest football tournament departs for kickoff in less than two years. As we are counting down the days until we put on our favorite jerseys and wave our nations’ flag with pride, we find ourselves at the mercy of the inefficient and run-down public transportation system we have in this country. 

The 2026 FIFA Men’s World Cup is set to be hosted by the United States, Mexico and Canada with 48 countries (including the host nations) competing in various qualification rounds to secure their spot in the tournament. With less than two years before the first whistle is blown, the United States is scrambling to come up with a plan to address this issue. However, there was an opportunity for the United States to do a test run of a summer soccer tournament, while combating the current issues of their public transportation system in a professional manner. 

This past summer, the United States hosted the CONMEBOL Copa América tournament on home soil as “part of a strategic partnership between CONMEBOL and CONCACAF to strengthen and develop the sport in both regions.” In Kansas City, a World Cup and COPA América host city, for fans, “[a] near-complete lack of public transportation links to Arrowhead Stadium meant that the highways surrounding the Truman Sports Complex where it resides were gridlocked before kickoff of the United States’ game against Uruguay.” Imagine spending thousands of dollars to see your country play at the most prestigious soccer tournament in the world, just for you to be sitting in traffic because the bus was running late. 

Across the Hudson River in nearby East Rutherford, New Jersey, fans who had an expectation that New Jersey would deliver on its public transportation system ended up being more disappointed when they arrived to games late due to lack of buses and being stuck on trains. This comes just a few months after FIFA President Gianni Infantino announced that MetLife Stadium will host the 2026  World Cup final. It is disappointing to see that a nation that was carefully vetted through FIFA to host the biggest international tournament in the world failed to deliver the basic necessity of providing transportation for the fans in a continental tournament. Considering that the Copa América was the one golden opportunity the U.S. had to prove itself, we can safely conclude that this tournament was a disaster for all public transportation users nationwide. 

Nevertheless, it is not new for the United States to have such a poor track record of providing sufficient public transportation. In a report by the American Society of Civil Engineers, an organization that represents thousands of civil engineers, they cited how due to “lack of federal support… our nation’s busiest passenger rail corridor, the Northeast Corridor, infrastructure-related issues caused 328,000 train-delay minutes, or the equivalent of roughly 700 Northeast Regional train trips from Boston, Massachusetts, to Washington, D.C.” It is a cause for concern that the most concentrated public transportation network that has three major cities––Boston, Philadelphia & New York/New Jersey––that are hosting 21 matches, have this many issues with their public transportation system. The issue of providing sufficient public transportation should be a priority for the local and state governments who are hosting the matches and for Congress who issues the funding to these states to get their public transit projects off the ground. 

In anticipation for the World Cup, Kansas City plans on using their highways to their advantage by expanding their bus network for fans attending the match. Meanwhile, across the Hudson River, Governor Phill Murphy and New Jersey Transit announced a plan that involves a new line connection between Secaucus and MetLife Stadium. Despite these efforts, the United States is still far behind on this matter, with the American Society of Civil Engineers giving the United States a D- in the public transportation category. Nonetheless, there is still a lot more we can do at the federal level to bring this issue to the forefront before it’s too late. 

The United States introduced a bill back in 2021 that addressed the issue of public transportation infrastructure. Senate Bill 2726 (Public Transportation Expansion Act), sponsored by Georgia Senator Jon Ossoff, authorizes the Department of Transportation to increase its funding on projects on public transportation systems, projects such as zero emission rapid bus lanes. With the passage of this bill in the Senate, cities like East Rutherford and Kansas City can get even more funding for their transportation projects, even going as far as providing an extra bus/shuttle line or extra service on their existing train network. 

With the countdown to the opening match just 621 days away, public transportation infrastructure has to be our main focus for a successful and memorable tournament. If not, FIFA will depart from the United States after the final match on July 19th, 2026 knowing they have hosted their last tournament on U.S. soil.

By James Brooks

 

A Massachusetts lawsuit against Exxon Mobil Corporation claims, among other things, that the company systematically deceives the public as to the risks posed by fossil fuel-driven climate change. On this issue of transparency and before the lawsuit, the City of Cambridge, Massachusetts pioneered the very first gas pump warning label. This “warming label” outlines the public health and climate change effects from burning gasoline and in 2020 became the very first such regulation in the United States. Independent from the U.S., the Country of Sweden came up with its own gas pump warning label in 2021. The Hawaii legislature has had a warming label bill since 2022, which has yet to pass, with a new likely sponsor in 2025, Senator Chris Lee. 

The fossil fuel industry knows it delivers an indispensable product. As noted by scholar Kari Norgaard, fossil fuels delivering “comfortable lifestyles” are politically connected to studies of privilege as they deliver safety and stability for people living in fossil fuel developed countries. Even in a climate emergency, argue scholars Magali Delmas and Vanessa Burbano, the fossil fuel industry operates in a comparably lax regulatory environment. They call it a “brown industry;” its core business practices are a continuous environmental hazard that produces fixed and increasing external costs to society. 

You could say the fossil fuel industry has a certain inviolable status in these countries. Where it plays a vital economic role, “fear of losing fossil privileges” occurs across an ideological spectrum and is politically and continually delaying meaningful efforts to reduce fossil fuel emissions. The industry is a strong, “silent” type, say Delmas and Burbano, that is until a few local and national governments wanted warming labels. These scholars observed the industry will get plenty “vocal,” though, when their core business interests are suddenly threatened. Driving Force Sweden, for instance, a fossil fuel industry trade organization, recently announced, unsurprisingly, that it opposes the Swedish program for “eco-labels” on gas pumps. Consistent with its powerful status, however, the trade group seems to be influencing the Swedish Energy Agency (SEA), which operates the program. Feeling threatened and girding itself, the Swedish Green Motorist Group behind the pump label law recently released a statement of support for the program in response. 

Driving claims that an evaluation of eco-labels by the SEA shows it is ineffective and thus doesn’t justify its cost. Oddly, SEA seems to be taking a fossil fuel trade group’s dubious assessment of the results seriously. SEA, for instance, didn’t ask the opinions of Dr. Stylianos Syropoulos and colleagues at Boston College, who are currently conducting an efficacy study on warming labels. Unlike Driving, Dr. Syropoulos said the SEA evaluation “shows the public supports the labels,” which, according to my own review, confirms already mainstream concerns about the climate and public health impacts of fossil fuels. People may fear losing their fossil fuels but they also fear fossil fuel-induced climate change. And with repeated exposure to an already popular message about the harms from fossil fuel, warming labels have the potential to tip the scales towards greater public buy-in; they can create a new focal point that gasoline is too risky to burn and begin to “increase perceived support” for efforts to decarbonize transportation. 

Warming labels on gas pumps, when cleaner alternatives are available, have the potential to reduce the status of fossil fuels. Gas is too risky to burn, as a new social baseline, may be a necessary pretext in any comprehensive effort to shift away from them. While research is ongoing, preliminary findings from the Boston College study appear to show that the labels increase perceptions that others in the community “disapprove of using fossil fuels for personal vehicles.” To permanently decarbonize transportation involves preemptive consensus-building among a largely apathetic-about-climate change driving public. That is, drivers themselves must agree upfront and together that fossil fuels are no longer worth burning, and that mitigating investments in low carbon transportation infrastructure are needed now. More precisely, sustained support towards decarbonizing the Massachusetts transportation system by 2050, is contingent on continuous public approval of this project and acceptance of some of the behavioral changes associated with it. 

But, as mentioned previously, the fossil fuel industry has influence. What the trade group did in Sweden, the Western States Petroleum Association did in Berkeley, CA back in 2014. Before the Berkeley City Council voted on warming labels—it never passed into law—“WiSPA” threatened to sue. Their show of force was enough to chill the legislative action for warming labels occurring all along the West Coast. In another example of this sway in 2016, a collaboration of Canadian fossil fuel interests rendered the first bylaw for the labels in the world, industry greenwash. A City of North Vancouver “partnership” with the consortium produced labels that messaged “caring concern” for the environment, and the status quo, so long as you used the fuel efficiently. 

Fossil fuel industry shenanigans continued with the 2023 Hawaii bill too. But the courts this year disrupted business as usual. The Hawaii Energy Marketing Association in 2023 testified, rather incoherently, that the labels “unfairly target a specific industry when other everyday decisions consumers make have an impact on the environment.” This doozy might have been enough to defer the bill then, and in 2024. But the Hawaii Circuit Court ruling against the Department of Transportation last year called HEMA’s bluff. The court said the agency violates the State Constitution’s public trust doctrine and right to a clean and healthful environment. It determined that the largest threat to a clean and healthy environment in Hawaii comes specifically from transportation fuel burning at the rate of 9.63 million metric tons of CO2 per year. 

While aviation in a tourist economy is the largest quotient, a not insignificant 3.53 million metric tons of CO2 is emitted by, you guessed it, the driving public. Perhaps inadvertently, the historic Navahine v. Hawaii Department of Transportation ruling focused attention on a consumer’s right to know and where any serious scheme to reduce emissions in ground transportation requires direct engagement with the people whose driving choices determine any of these reductions. The good news is that the public is particularly concerned about the public health effects from burning gasoline so labels that focus on that suggest the most direct way to engage them. But more materially, the lawsuit in Hawaii reveals a disconnect between the court precedent, the Hawaii Department of Transportation mandate to reach zero emissions in transportation by 2045, and the need to increase the driving public’s knowledge of these negative health effects. Doing so, according to the Boston College research, points to mobilizing consumers of gas in their key mitigating role. Smoking rates, for instance, that coincided with already existing concerns about the health effects from cigarette smoking, declined when cigarette warning labels began systematically educating the public. Moreover, as noted by University of Hawaii health communication expert Hye-ryeon Lee in her testimony for the Hawaii bill last year, “knowledge alone” about the dangers from gas burning doesn’t prompt action, but “repeated cues” about these dangers can. 

If we deduce that transportation emissions are determined by the choices of the driving public, warming labels are a natural extension of the Hawaii DOT lawsuit where it assumes greater investments in clean transportation infrastructure, subject to lasting public support. As evidenced by the initial research, the labels introducing a new social pressure to choose non-fossil sources of energy may interrupt a consumer’s entitlement to gasoline and, hence, the industry’s socio-political power. If we look at the incoming Trump Administration as the “vocal” embodiment of the fossil fuel industry, federal policies directed by an EPA and a ready Congress that will regulate it for planetary health and develop a required warming label, look unlikely. Which leaves state legislatures and municipal governments across America to fill in this leadership gap with their own regulations. An exemplary act of resistance to fossil fuel status and its anti-regulatory politics is the leadership demonstrated by the Cambridge City Council and Sweden. It’s obvious that other local and state governments emulating them will likely face full fossil fuel industry pique, not to mention significant constitutional hurdles. But what is also clear is that the industry fears the public capacity for the needed volte-face on gasoline that may come with the labels. It lies just beneath the surface.
